RibbonNativeAccess reads the native ribbon objects. src/dbtools.Core dbtools.Core.dll Safe execution, run scopes, call gates, transactions, settings, warnings, logging, banners, and the tool registry and loader. src/dbtools.Manifest Merged into Core The manifest.yml parser (net8.0), shared with the build tasks. src/dbtools.Presentation dbtools.Presentation.dll Stable WPF themes, controls, window shells and compiled tool resources. src/Tools/<Category>/<Tool> Tools/dbtools.<Tool>.dll One assembly for each tool. src/dbtools.Sandbox dbtools.Sandbox.exe Validates a staged product year and opens its tool windows outside the Revit process. See Sandbox Validator. Desktop projects target net10.0-windows ($(DBT_RevitTargetFramework)), and $(RevitYear) selects the Revit API references and output folder. Core and SGT also build for net10.0, without WPF or the Revit API, for portable pure tests. The Revit 2026 Design Automation appbundle targets net8.0-windows. Directory.Build.targets defines the compilation symbol REVIT2027_OR_GREATER for every project built with RevitYear 2027 or later; code that uses API new in Revit 2027 compiles only under that symbol. CONTRACTS Each rule names its check, if any. References. App references Core and Presentation. Core (net10.0-windows) references Presentation, dbtools.Manifest and the Revit API. Tools reference Core and Presentation. Presentation. Presentation uses WPF. It owns the merged HelixToolkit, Serilog and Microsoft.Extensions libraries in AssemblyMerges.props. It never references App, Core, a tool or the Revit API. BuildPolicyBehaviorTests and HelixMergeArtifactContractTests check parts of rules 1 and 2. Sandbox. The Sandbox compiles against Core and Presentation with Private="false", and loads them from the year folder that it validates. No third-party DLLs. build/Merging/AssemblyMerges.props merges each third-party runtime library into the assembly that owns it. The build checks its output against DistributionContract.ProductFiles. Tool assemblies. Tool projects set DBT_IsToolAssembly=true. The build stages them in Tools/ with a content-derived version, which ContentVersionTests checks. One tool folder. ToolAssemblyResolver.LoadAssembly loads only <folder of dbtools.dll>/Tools/<name>.dll, into the load context of dbtools.dll. ToolAssemblyResolverTests checks this. No load context of its own. dbtools creates no AssemblyLoadContext. Installed, it runs in the default context of Revit. The daemon uses ProductLoadContext for hosted tests and DevModeLoadContext for Dev Mode (Assembly Loading Contract). Themes per view. Each view merges the theme itself and leaves Application.Resources unchanged (Theme System). Fallback log. AppFallbackFailureLog.RecordFailure uses only the BCL, so it works before Core loads. FLOW Startup AddinEntry.OnStartup runs these steps: Idle check (AddinIdle). When DBTOOLS_DAEMON_REVIT_ROLE is set, the copy of dbtools.dll in the default context stays idle. It stores its path in the AppContext data dbtools-daemon.IdleAddin:dbtools and returns Succeeded, so the daemon can test its own copy. User data directory (AddinUserData). OnStartup reads DBT_USER_DATA_DIR once. An unset or empty value leaves AppPaths.BaseDir unchanged: %APPDATA%\dbtools, or the dbtools.AppPaths.BaseDir AppContext value when one is set. Any other value must be an absolute path to an existing directory that the process can write; its full path becomes that AppContext value. A value that fails these checks returns Failed before any runtime work, and OnShutdown then returns Succeeded at once. The failure names the variable, the value and the reason. It goes to Trace and to the startup failure dialog, which DBT_TEST_RUN_ID suppresses, and to no file. A set value never falls back to %APPDATA%\dbtools. Callback scope. AppStartupBoundary.Start enters ToolWindowCallbackScope, which suppresses ExecutionContext flow and sets contextual reflection to the dbtools.dll context. Start is not inlined, so no other product assembly loads before the idle check. Pending cleanup. AppLifecycleCoordinator.Start returns Failed while an earlier failed start still cleans up. Runtime. Startup reads the Revit year from VersionNumber. AppRuntimeFactory builds logging, services and the tool registrations, and AppRuntimeAccessor publishes them. Preparation. AppStartupPreparationWorkflow runs ValidateTheme, CreateDeferredStartupRunner, ComposeRibbon, PublishInitialStartupEffects and StartBackgroundStartup. The background task installs the main-window owner provider and attaches the hooks. Publication. Startup registers the failed-startup cleanup handler first, then the deferred handlers, and publishes the started state. The deferred handlers apply the deferred StartupContribution effects once the main window exists. A failure in steps 5 to 7 cleans up and returns Failed. A later background-task failure cleans up at the next Idling event. Tool registration ToolModuleCatalog.Discover reads the embedded manifests. For each moduleType, it loads the assembly with ToolAssemblyResolver and creates the ToolModule through its public parameterless constructor. It sorts the modules by order, then by type name. Any error stops startup. AppToolModuleRegistrar stages the settings, services, packs, hooks and ribbon tools of each module, and checks them. A manifest without moduleType adds ribbon tools only, through ToolModuleRibbonRegistrar. ToolRegistry.MergeFrom checks every internal name and lifecycle hook first, and changes nothing on a conflict. A ribbon button names its command by assembly path and class name. Without availabilityType, a command that implements IExternalCommandAvailability is its own availability class. ToolCommand does, and requires an active document by default. Command run ToolCommand.Execute enters ToolWindowCallbackScope and runs through ISafeExecutor. CommandContextFactory.CreateContext calls CommandPreflight.Validate before it opens a run scope. Preflight refuses the command if its panel is off, availability refuses it, or an active warning disables it. IAppRunScopeFactory opens a run scope with the command's profile. InlineUi runs on the Revit UI thread, and QueuedModeless queues work to it from a modeless window. The command returns Succeeded, or Cancelled after a refusal or a failure, so Revit shows no error dialog. See Revit Execution. DATA Item Holds App service provider Logging, settings, hooks, ISafeExecutor, the tool registry and the ribbon state Run scope IRevitRunScope, IRevitCallGate, ITransactionRunner and ITransactionGroupService (RevitServiceCollectionExtensions), opened through IAppRunScopeFactory AppPaths.BaseDir: %APPDATA%\dbtools\, or the DBT_USER_DATA_DIR directory settings.<year>.json, Logs\ and Cache\ System temporary directory (Path.GetTempPath()) Transient files with unique names that ElevationTags, FoundationTags and RecordSet try to delete after use. TMP and TEMP relocate it. DIAGNOSTICS Logs\dbtools.Fallback.log below AppPaths.BaseDir holds failures from before logging starts, such as a bad Revit year, and failures that the logger cannot record. The log names a failed startup phase. After a refused DBT_USER_DATA_DIR, records go to Trace only. AppStartupFailurePresenter shows a dialog unless DBT_TEST_RUN_ID is set. TESTS ./test.sh test --tool APP ./test.sh test --tool APP --scope local -y 2026 ./test.sh test --tool CORE ./test.sh test --tool CORE --scope local -y 2026 Selection Covers APP pure Idle check, fallback log, startup effects, failure presenter, ribbon planning APP local AddinEntry, lifecycle, module registration, ribbon CORE pure Discovery, tool loading, safe execution CORE local Registry, preflight SEE ALSO Assembly Loading Contract, Build Pipeline, Test Pipeline, App, Core

developer-guide/architecture/revit-execu.title: Revit Execution and Progress Overlay | dbtools
developer-guide/architecture/revit-execu.summary: Revit Execution and Progress Overlay dbtools runs all Revit API work through a call gate, inside a run scope that each command, modeless session or test owns. Tool windows report long operations through the progress overlay. This page owns the design of run scopes, call gates, transaction services and the progress overlay. dbtools.Core describes the rest of the Core library and its source folders. Command entry ToolCommand (src/dbtools.Core/Tools/Commands/ToolCommand.cs) is the base class of every Revit command. Its public Execute runs the command body inside ISafeExecutor and gives the protected RunAsync hook one owning CommandContext; see ToolCommand for the API. Command subclasses resolve services from ICommandContext. Its base interface IAppRunScope exposes the scope's RevitRunScope and Resolve<T>(). A feature that owns a window composes ToolWindowFactory and calls CreateModal for an IModalToolWindowSession with ShowDialog/HideForPick, or CreateModeless for an IModelessToolWindowSession with Show. The session owns the reflection scope and the window's retirement. An expected refusal throws SafeExecutionRefusedException with a reason for the user. SafeExecutor then returns SafeExecutionStatus.Refused, with no exception diagnostics. SafeExecutionRefusalReporter shows a Warning banner, which writes the one Warning log entry; an execution without a banner logs [Refused] {Name}: {Message}. ToolCommand returns Revit Result.Cancelled for a refusal and for a failure. An unexpected exception writes Error diagnostics and shows an Error banner with Details. Run scopes App composition (AppServiceProviderFactory) registers IAppRunScopeFactory with the Core implementation AppRunScopeFactory. CommandContextFactory calls Create(UIApplication, AppRunScopeProfile). The factory selects the call gate for the profile, constructs RevitRunScope, and returns the concrete AppRunScope, which owns scoped service resolution, its IRevitRunScope and disposal. Construction and disposal keep the primary failure, attempt every owned cleanup step and report further cleanup failures in order. Profile Call gate Use InlineUi (default) InlineRevitCallGate Modal commands and daemon-hosted Revit automation that already run on the Revit UI thread. QueuedModeless QueuedRevitCallGate Modeless tool windows and long workflows that must queue Revit API work to the UI thread through the service root's RevitCallGateTask. A tool selects its profile through RunProfile in its manifest; ToolRegistration uses InlineUi when none is given. IRevitRunScope owns the UIApplication, the call gate, document access and disposal. Transaction services are scoped registrations, resolved with Resolve<T>() on IAppRunScope or ICommandContext. public interface IRevitRunScope : IDisposable { UIApplication UIApplication { get; } IRevitCallGate CallGate { get; } UIDocument GetActiveUiDocument(); Document GetActiveDocument(); Document GetVerifiedActiveDocument(Document expectedDocument, string? context = null); } A consumer that keeps its launch document calls GetVerifiedActiveDocument(...). The run scope rejects an invalid expected or active document and requires matching DocumentSessionKey values before it returns the active document. RevitServiceCollectionExtensions registers only the Revit-scoped run-scope access, the call gate and the transaction services. The App composition root registers the Revit task, IAppRunScopeFactory, safe execution, command preflight and the command context services. Revit task Each App service root owns one RevitCallGateTask, the ExternalEvent host that queued gates schedule through. AppServiceProviderFactory registers it as a singleton that is created on first request, with ILogger<RevitCallGateTask>, and registers Func<IRevitCallGateTask>, which returns the task of the same root. Registration creates no ExternalEvent. After synchronous preparation, startup resolves the task on the Revit main thread and captures it in AppStartupOwnership. Shutdown retires and disposes that task before it disposes the service root. AppRunScopeFactory, HookHost, ContextualRibbonRuntime and the Foundation Tags update workflow receive the provider. They call it only when they build a QueuedRevitCallGate: a QueuedModeless run scope, a ViewActivated hook attachment or rollback, a contextual ribbon UI call, or the selection actions of an update result. An InlineUi run scope does not resolve the task. A gate keeps the task it was built with. After that generation retires, a new queued call completes canceled and does not reach a replacement task. A provider called after its root is disposed throws ObjectDisposedException. Call gates IRevitCallGate is the single entry point for Revit API access. It runs synchronous callbacks on the Revit UI thread. Revit API calls outside the call gate can raise invalid-context exceptions or break UI-thread rules. public interface IRevitCallGate { bool InGate { get; } bool RunsInline { get; } Task<T> RunAsync<T>(Func<UIApplication, T> work, CancellationToken ct = default, RevitCallGateMode mode = RevitCallGateMode.Auto); Task RunAsync(Action<UIApplication> work, CancellationToken ct = default, RevitCallGateMode mode = RevitCallGateMode.Auto); } Mode Behavior Auto Run inline when the caller already has a gate context; otherwise queue through the owned ExternalEvent host. ForceQueue Always queue through the owned ExternalEvent, in a later turn. The inline gate rejects it with ContextUnavailableException. InlineRevitCallGate(UIApplication) runs delegates immediately on the Revit UI thread with the supplied application. Modal commands use it. QueuedRevitCallGate(IRevitCallGateTask, ILogger) schedules the callback through the Revit task it receives. RunsInline is true when every accepted callback runs synchronously inside the calling API turn: true for InlineRevitCallGate, false for QueuedRevitCallGate, also while a nested Auto call runs inline. A decorator forwards the value of its inner gate. It grants no API authority and does not describe the current InGate state. SGT's modal session and GM's Commit Review modal session read it instead of the concrete gate type. QueuedRevitCallGate requires a Revit task and an ILogger; RevitCallGateTask requires an ILogger. A missing argument is a construction error. The active UIApplication, the queued-gate depth and the Revit-test depth are internal scoped state. QueuedRevitCallGate owns the queued and test scopes; RevitRunScope owns its application context token. Every scope restores the exact previous value, and a repeated disposal does nothing. Delegate admission Admission is synchronous and runs before the gate validates the API context or schedules anything. Keep asynchronous workflows outside the gate and make in-gate delegates synchronous: await _gate.RunAsync(app => { // Revit API work here (synchronous only) return true; }); Every member of an Action invocation list is checked for an async state machine, so an async void action is rejected. A delegate whose result type is Task, Task<T>, ValueTask or ValueTask<T>, including nullable ValueTask, is rejected. A multicast result delegate with a reference result type is rejected, because ordinary multicast dispatch exposes only the last return value. After invocation, a reference-typed result gets a runtime Task/ValueTask check, which also finds interface-typed Task and boxed ValueTask values. Custom awaiter structs are not detected. Sources: src/dbtools.Core/Revit/Execution/CallGate/{CallGateDelegateValidator,InlineRevitCallGate,QueuedRevitCallGate,RevitCallGateTask,RevitCallGateTaskQueue}.cs. API-context admission RevitCallGateApiContext.IsActive requires the Revit dispatcher thread and an explicit API scope. It reads this state without calling Revit. The scope lasts for the current synchronous callback. The ref struct scope ends before an asynchronous continuation resumes outside the callback. Revit entry Scope owner Tool commands ToolCommand.ExecuteCore Add-in startup AppLifecycleCoordinator.Start Add-in shutdown with a published lifecycle state AppLifecycleCoordinator.Shutdown ApplicationInitialized AppDeferredStartupSubscription.OnApplicationInitialized Idling AppLifecycleIdlingRegistration.RunCallback and PrerequisiteRetryCoordinator.RunRetryTick ViewActivated ViewActivationHookDispatcher.BeginDispatchHandlers SelectionChanged ContextualRibbonSelectionChangeController.BeginSelectionChanged ExternalEvent RevitCallGateTask.Execute and ContextualRibbonEditEventHandler.Execute Current returns the scope's UIApplication when available. A nested scope without a UIApplication inherits the enclosing scope's application. Startup and shutdown receive UIControlledApplication and enter without a UIApplication. If the scope has no application, the Revit task uses its own known application. If neither supplies one, queued work gets it in the next ExternalEvent callback. An application reference alone grants no authority. Revit still enforces the restrictions of the active callback. Document change handlers update the document stamp directly. A progress-overlay paint frame suspends API access for work dispatched by that frame. IsActive is false, Current is null, and the inline gate refuses calls in the paint frame itself. A nested WPF dispatcher loop uses the enclosing callback's scope. The paint frame suspends API access again when the nested loop exits. A callback owned by another add-in runs without dbtools API authority until it enters a dbtools callback. Use a queued gate and return control to Revit before waiting for the result. A synchronous wait on the Revit thread can prevent the queued callback from running. An inline gate refuses an unscoped call. Enter is internal. RevitCallGateApiContextEntryContractTests checks the compiled call sites and scope constructor and rejects native ExternalEvent references in API context methods. InlineRevitCallGate may enter a nested scope after it verifies thread and API access. Queued turns Each native Execute turn of the queued gate runs, in FIFO order, every item that was waiting when the turn started. N waiting calls cost one Revit round trip. Items queued during a turn wait for the next turn. After the first item, a turn starts no new item once its 50 ms budget (RevitCallGateTask.DrainBudget) is used. A failed or canceled item completes its own task; the turn continues with the next item. An item that leaves a transaction open in any document ends the turn. Revit discards what a callback leaves open only when the callback returns, so the next item must run in a later turn. An item that creates a transaction group through RevitTransactionGroups.Begin also ends the turn. Nested Auto calls run inline. ForceQueue defers to a later turn. A caller that needs several reads for one user action makes them in one RunAsync body, or starts independent calls together so that one turn runs them all. A transaction group without an open transaction is not visible to the open-transaction check. Production code therefore creates every TransactionGroup through RevitTransactionGroups.Begin(document, name, validateStart). The factory calls RevitCallGateTurnBoundary.EndAfterCurrentCall(), so the current turn ends when the running call returns, then constructs and starts the group and disposes it if the start fails. The build contract suite (TransactionGroupTurnBoundaryContractTests) inspects the compiled production assemblies and rejects TransactionGroup construction outside that factory. A caller on the Revit thread, outside Execute and outside a progress-overlay paint frame, raises at once. A worker posts its raise to the Revit dispatcher at Normal priority. Work left after a turn raises after Execute returns. A raise received during a paint frame is posted after the frame and the outermost API scope have exited. A nested dispatcher loop keeps the usual raise behavior for work that has no pending raise. Pending calls share a raise. A failed or aborted post faults the waiting calls and logs the failure. Autodesk says Revit invokes the handler “when there is an available Idling time cycle”. Autodesk External Events guide Denied and TimedOut raise results keep the queue and retry with a backoff from 50 ms, doubling to at most 500 ms, for at most 5 seconds (RevitCallGateRaiseRetry). When that time expires, the waiting batch faults; the scheduler still accepts new work. Each turn feeds a Debug summary with the prefix [CallGate/Turns]. It reports turns and calls, maximum queue depth, queue-to-raise time, the Raise-to-Execute gap, Execute duration, native Raise duration and results, and refused-raise retries. Queue-to-raise time starts when the oldest waiting call enters the queue and ends when its accepted native Raise starts. The summary is written when a turn leaves the queue empty, at most once per second, or after 10 s of a queue that stays busy. Turns inside the one-second interval are reported with the next activity. Each call records its queue, start and finish times in the caller's RevitCallGateActionTiming. Presentation owns the timing state so a captured execution context holds only stable types. SafeExecutor begins a timing for each run and logs its totals at Information level (see Core). Every RevitCallGateTask uses the same process clock. Retirement cancels the posted raise, stops and detaches the retry timer, releases queued delegates and disposes the native event. Dropped tasks never complete, so a worker that waits synchronously on one hangs. Cleanup after a failed startup cancels the tasks instead, because Revit and its callers are still running. Transactions Resolve transaction services from the command scope: context.Resolve<ITransactionRunner>() and context.Resolve<ITransactionGroupService>(). RevitServiceCollectionExtensions registers both as scoped services on the scope's IRevitCallGate. ITransactionRunner public interface ITransactionRunner { Task RunInActiveDocumentAsync(string name, Action<RevitTransactionContext> action, CancellationToken ct = default); Task<T> RunInActiveDocumentAsync<T>(string name, Func<RevitTransactionContext, T> action, CancellationToken ct = default); Task RunInDocumentAsync(Document doc, string name, Action<RevitTransactionContext> action, CancellationToken ct = default); Task<T> RunInDocumentAsync<T>(Document doc, string name, Func<RevitTransactionContext, T> action, CancellationToken ct = default); } Delegates receive RevitTransactionContext, which carries the UIApplication and the Document. TransactionRunner runs on IRevitCallGate and applies the synchronous delegate admission before it enters the gate or starts a transaction. The runtime awaitable check for a reference-typed result runs inside the transaction body, so an awaitable result rolls the transaction back before commit. If doc.IsModifiable (a transaction is already open), it uses a SubTransaction; otherwise it starts a Transaction. It refuses to start a transaction on one document while another document is modifiable. It attaches TransactionFailurePreprocessor, which suppresses non-critical Revit warnings. Work that calls RevitTransactionContext.DeleteOnlyWarnings(failureDefinitionIds) lets the transaction delete only the listed warnings; any other warning rolls it back like an error and is reported as Warning <GUID>: <description>. A subtransaction refuses that call, because its transaction handles its warnings. TransactionRunner enters the call gate and resolves the target document through TransactionBoundary (RunAsync, GetActiveDocument and EnsureNoCrossDocNesting). TransactionExecutor owns the Transaction or SubTransaction lifecycle and names an unnamed transaction dbtools Transaction. The static status validators of TransactionBoundary turn an unexpected start, commit or group-finalization status into TransactionFailureException; TransactionExecutor and TransactionGroupSession call them, and TransactionGroupSession names an unnamed group dbtools Apply Group. await _transactionRunner.RunInActiveDocumentAsync("Create Wall", context => { Wall.Create(context.Document, curve, levelId, false); }); var wallId = await _transactionRunner.RunInActiveDocumentAsync("Create Wall", context => Wall.Create(context.Document, curve, levelId, false).Id); Failure handling TransactionRunner collects failures through transaction or subtransaction disposal before returning a result. The first operation failure stops further work. Existing work/rollback aggregates precede any disposal failure. A single failure keeps its identity, type and original stack. Multiple failures propagate in an ordered aggregate. A disposal failure after commit does not fail the call: TransactionDisposal logs it at Error with the transaction name through SerilogStaticLogger, and the call returns the committed result. TransactionFailurePreprocessor.AttachToTransaction sets clear-after-rollback before failure processing starts. Revit holds a stable RevitCallbackRelay (Presentation) that forwards to the preprocessor. After a transaction ends, Revit can keep native copies of the failure handling options until it next pumps, and a Dev Mode reload proves the old generation unreachable before that. Production code therefore declares the preprocessor before its transaction and attaches it with AttachTo after Start, so the transaction is disposed, and rolled back if needed, before Dispose drops the preprocessor from the relay; its records stay readable. For the same reason, copy-paste options get a constant relay (RevitCallbackRelay.Constant) as the duplicate type names handler. Hand Revit a relay, not a reloadable object, for any callback that Revit can keep after the call. A warning is reported as suppressed only after Revit deletes it. A blocking failure, or a fault in a failure accessor, records a blocking diagnostic and requests rollback. An accessor fault keeps the caught exception, which becomes the InnerException of the TransactionFailureException (an AggregateException when several accessors failed). An attachment fault propagates before commit; the preprocessor does not change rollback options inside the failure callback. The preprocessor keeps one TransactionFailureRecord per message it reads: severity, description, failure definition GUID, failing element IDs and whether the message rolled the transaction back. A fault while reading the failing element IDs is added to AccessorFaults and does not change how the message resolves. A runner built with new TransactionRunner(gate, logger) logs every record and every accessor fault at Warning after the commit; the one-argument constructor logs nothing. GM's apply runners use the logging form. TransactionFailureException is the public diagnostic for a transaction that did not reach Committed. Its constructors are internal to Core. Callers read the transaction name, final status, warnings, blocking failure text and failure-definition identities from its properties. BlockingFailureDefinitionIds keeps the IDs in the order Revit reported them, duplicates included, and BlockingFailureDefinitionGuids holds their GUIDs in the same order. The exception implements ITransactionFailureDefinitionSource, which exposes only the GUID list, so code without the Revit API can read it. Core does not classify the GUIDs; GM's GroupEditErrorMatcher matches Revit's four group-edit failures. A posted blocking failure rolls back a runner-managed transaction and raises this exception with the transaction name and the blocking diagnostic. Tool write boundaries map this exception and Revit refusal exceptions to their own typed failures and keep the original exception as the inner cause. Sources: src/dbtools.Core/Revit/Transactions/{TransactionRunner,TransactionExecutor,TransactionDisposal,TransactionBoundary,TransactionFailurePreprocessor}.cs. Transaction groups ITransactionGroupService makes several transactions on the active document one Revit undo entry. It is the manual lifecycle; the caller owns the try/finally around FinalizeAsync, in the workflow that knows whether to commit or roll back. public interface ITransactionGroupService { bool IsActive { get; } TransactionGroupOutcome LastFinalizationOutcome { get; } Task BeginAsync(string name, CancellationToken ct = default); Task FinalizeAsync(TransactionGroupFinalization finalization, CancellationToken ct = default); Task<bool> IsGroupHealthyAsync(CancellationToken ct = default); } If the document is already modifiable, BeginAsync creates no group, IsActive becomes true, and FinalizeAsync only resets state. LastFinalizationOutcome reports Committed or RolledBack when Revit confirms that result, including when a later cleanup step fails. It is Unconfirmed before confirmation and resets when a new session begins. FinalizeAsync accepts only TransactionGroupFinalization.Commit (assimilate) and Rollback; another value fails before the inactive-session check. Finalization always clears the active group state and attempts disposal of the owned group. If the operation and the cleanup both fail, the operation failure comes first in an ordered aggregate. Revit rolls back a group that is still open when the API callback that started it returns, and RevitTransactionGroups.Begin ends the queued turn after the current call. Separate BeginAsync and FinalizeAsync calls therefore keep one group only on an InlineUi gate inside one callback, as the modal Super Girt Tool (SGT) and Transfer Drafting Views (TDV) commands use them. Queued modeless work uses IAtomicTransactionGroup.RunAsync(name, work, keep, ct), which TransactionGroupService also implements; GM commit review constructs it directly for its gate. In one gate call it begins the group, runs the work, then assimilates the group when keep(result) is true and rolls it back otherwise. The group is one Revit undo entry also under the queued gate. An exception, or a cancellation seen at any point before finalization (also after the work returns), rolls the group back and propagates. A document that already has an open transaction is refused before any work, because the group would own nothing to roll back. The work must complete inside the callback, where its gate calls run inline. Work still pending when the callback returns is canceled and the group is rolled back. The outcome is classified by the group status Revit reports: only RolledBack counts as discarded and only Committed as kept. Any other status throws TransactionGroupOutcomeUnknownException, and the caller must not report the work as discarded. Progress overlay Hosts Host tool views through ToolWindowFactory.CreateModal or CreateModeless. The typed sessions share the IToolWindowSession lifecycle. The modal and modeless shells expose the WPF owner. Core installs WindowInitializer before the XAML loads and retires its state with the session. Bind an overlay to its window with ProgressOverlay.For(window, logger), on the owner's UI thread. State, dispatcher affinity and diagnostics stay tied to that window. The logger is required. WindowProgressOverlayCapability (WindowProgressOverlayCapability.Hosts.cs) is the only registry from Window to overlay state and visual host. There is no ambient or process-global host. ProgressOverlay.Operations.cs holds the public lifecycle API. ProgressOverlayRunWorkflow.cs owns RunAsync(...): the show policy, the linked cancellation source, cancel observation and hide sequencing. ProgressOverlayDelayedHideScheduler keeps the dispatcher operation it posts and observes every outcome. It clears the pending hide only when the completing operation owns the current cancellation source, so an aborted or faulted stale operation cannot clear a replacement hide. Before a tool modal or file picker opens, Core finishes the owner overlay's pending minimum-duration hide. IProgressOverlay Member Behavior Show(title, cancelable) Shows the overlay and resets the cancellation state. Update(status, progress01) Sets status text and progress in [0,1]. A null argument leaves that value unchanged. A non-finite progress value throws ArgumentOutOfRangeException before status or progress changes. Finite values are clamped to [0,1]. AsProgress() Returns a synchronous IProgress<(string message, double? progress01)> sink that calls Update. Use it for progress reports made during inline UI-thread work. UpdateStep(current, total, description, progress01) Sets the status to Step X/Y: {description}. Scope(title, cancelable) Shows the overlay and attempts a paint before returning. Nested scopes restore the parent title and cancelability. CancelRequested Thread-safe snapshot of the Cancel button state. RequestCancel() Sets CancelRequested. Hide() Hides the overlay and clears transient state. RunAsync(title, work, cancelable, options, ct) Shows the overlay and attempts a paint before non-cancelable work starts, then runs work with an overlay lifecycle and cancellation bridge. A second run on the same window while one is active throws InvalidOperationException. ProgressOverlay marshals public calls to its owner's WPF dispatcher. Do not change overlay state directly from a background thread. Pure and view-model tests can use a simple IProgressOverlay double. Rendering The overlay belongs to the owner's visual tree and disables the underlying content while visible. A status change requests an immediate paint. Progress-only requests are limited to one frame per 85 ms. A paint runs one frame on the owner's dispatcher. The filters pass client-area mouse moves and left-button messages inside the visible Cancel button, plus WM_MOUSELEAVE and WM_NCMOUSELEAVE. They drop other mouse, pointer, touch, keyboard, system-key, and system-command window messages addressed to windows on the thread. A nested WPF dispatcher loop receives input normally. After a dropped button or key release, the paint frame sends WM_CANCELMODE to the window that has mouse capture as it exits. Posted messages such as WM_TIMER, WM_COMMAND, WM_PAINT, and application messages to Revit's windows pass through during a frame. Dispatcher work at the frame's exit priority or higher can also run. The exit priority is Background for cancelable overlays and Render for non-cancelable overlays. This work can execute inside the current Revit callback without API access (IsActive is false). WPF's WISP touch and pen stack queues Input-priority dispatcher operations. Those operations can run in a cancelable frame because the filter examines window messages. A non-cancelable overlay exits at WPF Render priority. A cancelable overlay runs through Input priority so a Cancel click can set CancelRequested during inline work. A separate Render marker records whether the paint priority ran. A 20 ms deadline stops the frame between messages. A callback already running can finish. A missed Render marker logs at most one warning per overlay showing. An update made in the paint frame changes the overlay without opening another paint frame. An overlay in a nested WPF dispatcher loop can paint. The pump identifies nested WPF loops by dispatcher frame depth. A paint frame that starts on a nonmodal thread also detects a transition to modal state. On an already-modal thread, only a depth change identifies a nested loop. Native dialogs such as MessageBox can leave both values unchanged. The paint restrictions on API access, queued raises, and nested painting remain in effect during such a loop. App startup checks that WPF provides Dispatcher._frameDepth. If the field is unavailable, startup fails with the field name and the installed WPF WindowsBase version in the diagnostic. The dispatcher tracks the active paint frame until it exits, including when Dev Mode retires its dispatcher operations. The pump releases the frame before resuming work deferred by it. WPF dispatchers keep their usual route for foreign exceptions and exceptions an earlier subscriber handled. For an unhandled dbtools exception in the paint frame, the pump marks it handled and requests frame exit. This lets the callback return through its window procedure. Errors in nested WPF loops use the usual WPF route. A separate dispatcher operation reports captured dbtools errors and dbtools errors that escape the paint frame. Multiple failures are reported together, once per exception instance. Other UnhandledException subscribers can see the original notification during painting and the DispatcherCallbackException during delivery. The window error boundary presents the deferred report after inline work yields. If the dispatcher aborts delivery, the scheduler logs the report. Cancellation Use RunAsync(...) for long operations. ProgressOverlayRunWorkflow observes CancelRequested, cancels a linked token source and passes the work delegate a token that fires on cancel. After Show(...) resets the cancellation state, the cancel watcher starts before the work begins. SGT analysis (AnalysisSessionWorkflow), SGT placement (PlacementWorkflow) and GM commit review (CommitReviewApplyOverlayWorkflow) use RunAsync. A workflow that drives its own Scope(...) reads CancelRequested and bridges it to its own cancellation. TDV transfer does this: its reporter returns Overlay.CancelRequested as IsCancellationRequested. using (Overlay.Scope("Transferring Drafting Views", cancelable: true)) { result = await _session.ApplySelectionAsync(items, reporter, CancellationToken.None); } Progress values Tools report IProgress<(string message, double? progress01)>: a status message and an optional fraction in [0,1]. MonotonicProgressAdapter (src/dbtools.Core/Progress/Aggregation) wraps such a reporter and forwards non-decreasing values clamped to [0,1]. A null fraction forwards the status and does not change the tracked value. A non-finite fraction throws ArgumentOutOfRangeException and does not change the tracked value. Create one adapter per operation. Tool Progress source Overlay mapping GM MappingPlanExecutor reports per-writer progress (writerIndex / writerCount); MappingApplyState.ReportProgress(message, progress01) reports within a writer. CommitReviewApplyWorkflow wraps the reporter in MonotonicProgressAdapter; CommitReviewApplyOverlayWorkflow updates the overlay. TDV The transfer executor reports per-view stage percentages (0, 10, 25, 35, 60, 85, 100). TdvWindowViewModel.UpdateTransferOverlayProgress maps them through six weighted stages and never decreases. SGT PlacementExecutor.PlaceAsync / UpdateAsync report wall-level and sub-step progress. PlacementWorkflow wraps the overlay in MonotonicProgressAdapter. Record Set ExecutionPlanExecutor.ExecuteAsync takes an Action<int> percentage and an Action<string> log. PlanExecutionWorkflow combines the last percentage with each log message in one overlay update. Common failures Dispatcher errors or missing state: an overlay call on a window that Core WindowInitializer did not initialize, or a change that bypasses the overlay API. Invalid Revit API context: Revit API calls outside IRevitCallGate, or async delegates inside the gate.

developer-guide/architecture/sandbox-val.title: Sandbox Validator | dbtools
developer-guide/architecture/sandbox-val.summary: Sandbox Validator NAME sandbox validator - check a product year and construct its WPF windows SYNOPSIS Source src/dbtools.Sandbox/ Program dbtools.Sandbox.exe Entry dbtools.Sandbox.App.Startup.SandboxEntry dbtools.Sandbox.exe [--dist-dir DIR] [--headless --revit-reference-dir DIR] DESCRIPTION Sandbox validates one product year in a standalone x64 Windows process. See dbtools.Sandbox for interactive previews. Option Effect --dist-dir DIR Selects a directory named for its Revit year or a root that contains year directories. For a root, Sandbox chooses the highest supported year that contains dbtools.dll. --headless Runs validation and exits. The default mode opens the window catalog. --revit-reference-dir DIR Supplies the Revit metadata references. This option is required in headless mode and reserved for that mode. The path options accept --option DIR and --option=DIR. The default distribution root is .artifacts/dist/Release/ in the checkout that contains the executable under .artifacts/sandbox/. Outside that layout, Sandbox resolves the default relative to the working directory. CONTRACTS A candidate contains dbtools.addin, dbtools.dll, dbtools.Core.dll, dbtools.Presentation.dll and a flat Tools/ directory. SandboxCandidate rejects unexpected root DLLs and mismatched assembly names. See Assembly Loading Contract. Both modes require the matching Revit installation. RevitRuntimeResolver uses ricaun.Revit.Installation to locate it. It checks AdWindows.dll, RevitAPI.dll, RevitAPIUI.dll and UIFramework.dll against the selected references. Interactive mode uses the installed files as its references. FLOW SandboxEntry resolves and checks the candidate before WPF starts. It loads Presentation, Core and App from the candidate into the default assembly load context. SandboxDistributionContext resolves each tool assembly from the candidate when needed. HeadlessValidationWorkflow checks add-in metadata, theme resources and the catalog. ManifestValidator checks tool modules, command and availability types, and icon resources. ToolWindowValidator opens each manifest window with its design-time view model and checks layout, tab changes and row details. SandboxCatalog also supplies alert requests, VTC alert bodies and color picker, Settings packs, notification banners, progress overlays, and the Change Review, Manage Items, Revit Link Settings, and Duplicate Type Mapping dialogs. Manifest and contributed cases use production sessions with sample inputs. Modeless sessions open with Show. Modal sessions open with ShowDialog and run a posted validation callback inside the dialog loop before closing with a dialog result. Settings uses sample library file years and spot elevation types. The FoundationTags pack requires the active Revit project and is excluded from this check. The validator subscribes to each window's production error path. Manifest windows and contributed cases with an error boundary report handled errors. Notification banners report errors through Dispatcher.UnhandledException. The expanded notification stack check observes layout updates at ApplicationIdle until the banner reaches its height cap and the vertical scrollbar is visible. The check has a 15-second deadline and reports the measured height, cap and scroll state on failure. The validator checks WPF binding errors while the window and each selected tab are loaded and the dispatcher has reached ApplicationIdle. Error 2 clears when the same binding expression reaches Active with a value. During retirement, the validator uses that expression's recorded loaded state. Every other binding error fails validation. The validator waits for ApplicationIdle after close. A missing required boundary, a window error, or a close or retirement failure also fails validation. After the window checks, the workflow rejects any loaded Revit host assembly from the reference set. It closes remaining windows and disposes the candidate's window runtime. Build the matching Sandbox executable before validating a staged year. These commands validate a promoted Revit 2026 distribution from the checkout root on Windows. pwsh -NoProfile -File build.ps1 BuildSandbox -y 2026 .\.artifacts\sandbox\Release\2026\net10.0-windows\dbtools.Sandbox.exe --headless ` --dist-dir .artifacts\dist\Release\2026 ` --revit-reference-dir 'C:\Program Files\Autodesk\Revit 2026' DATA From a clean checkout, PackageSandboxValidationInput builds a Release candidate and Sandbox for both supported years. It writes validate-dist-<sha256>.zip under .artifacts/.staging/<build-id>/native-validation-input/. The archive carries the candidate, Sandbox and Revit reference files under candidate/<year>/, sandbox/<year>/net10-0-windows/ and revit-refs/<year>/. Its root manifest.json records the payload paths and SHA-256 hashes. Run DIST before staging another candidate. StageDistributionCandidate tries to delete earlier staging directories and their archives. DIAGNOSTICS Headless mode returns 0 on success and 1 on failure. Startup errors and the validation result go to standard error. In a DIST run, SandboxLauncher includes that output in the failing test message. Message Meaning and action Unable to infer Revit year from dist dir: '<path>'. RevitRuntimeResolver.ResolveRuntimeDirOrThrow raises this when the final directory name fails to parse as a year. Use a year directory such as 2026. Revit <year> install was not found. Install Revit <year>. Match the installed Revit year to the candidate year. Headless Sandbox validation requires --revit-reference-dir. Pass a directory with the four Revit metadata references for the candidate year. Tool UI validation failed: Find the window ID, XAML resource and view model in the Sandbox standard error output. TESTS WindowsAcceptanceTests provides ValidatesTheStagedCandidateFor2026 and ValidatesTheStagedCandidateFor2027. Each DIST request runs one year in its own process and verifies the complete archive. DevModeGenerationProbe from dbtools-daemon.DevMode.Testing loads that year's candidate. The test opens and closes each SandboxCatalog window and requires the generation to retire. It then runs the staged Sandbox with --headless against the candidate and its archived Revit references. See Distribution acceptance. SEE ALSO dbtools.Sandbox, Build Pipeline, Sandbox Integration, Test Pipeline

developer-guide/architecture/structural-.title: Structural Preview | dbtools
developer-guide/architecture/structural-.summary: Structural Preview dbtools.Presentation.StructuralPreview is the stable WPF host for the structural 3D preview shared by the Extreme Roof Framing Tool (ERFT) and the Super Girt Tool (SGT). A tool adapter supplies immutable scene data and receives pointer events. The host owns the Helix viewport, effects manager, camera, navigation, materials, hit testing, tooltip, overlay markers and cleanup. Helix and SharpDX are merged into Presentation as internal types; no tool assembly or raw view names them. ERFT and SGT register the presenter's disposal with their tool-window sessions. The component has no Core, App or tool-assembly dependency. Its public scene records contain only immutable arrays, System.Numerics values, strings, integers and scalar values. Attach and dispose Call StructuralPreview3DFactory.Attach on the viewport host dispatcher. The ContentControl must be empty. The optional overlay canvas must use the same dispatcher. The returned IStructuralPreview3D owns one viewport and one effects manager. All presenter methods and disposal are synchronous UI-thread operations. Attach returns a disabled presenter with the load error as its reason when Helix libraries cannot be loaded. The disabled presenter still validates and copies supplied scene and emphasis data, reports its status reason, returns false from projection, and can be disposed repeatedly. For an available presenter, Dispose removes viewport, camera, owner-window, timer and input handlers; closes the tooltip; removes only the overlay children created by this presenter; disposes owned scene elements, viewport and effects manager; clears scene data and subscriber events; and clears the host content only when that content is still the viewport owned by this presenter. Cleanup is synchronous and does not post a dispatcher frame. Disposal clears subscriptions before cleanup, so it publishes zero presenter events during or after disposal. Repeated disposal is safe. Scene data and picks SetScene validates and deep-copies the supplied records and arrays. The caller may then release or reuse its own objects. Equal mesh geometry keeps existing Helix models; geometry or appearance changes update the rendered decorations and materials, while bounds or exterior-normal changes update camera state. Mesh Opacity supplies the material alpha and overrides the alpha byte in Argb. Line sets multiply their ARGB alpha by Opacity. Selection and hover colors preserve the mesh opacity. Mesh picking is independent of emphasis. A mesh is eligible for a hit only when its supplied IsPickable value is true; context meshes can therefore be pickable or non-pickable independently of their material role. A floor is supplied as scene geometry, normally a context mesh with IsPickable: false. Line sets and non-pickable meshes do not produce mesh hits. A missed hit has null mesh ID, null context ID and null world point. A hit's mesh and context hits are resolved independently: each is the nearest eligible hit for its role. MeshId is the nearest member ID, or null when there is no member hit; ContextId is the nearest context ID independently. WorldPoint is the nearest member hit point when one exists, otherwise the context hit point, so a context-only hit has a null mesh ID and a context world point. The event also carries WPF screen coordinates relative to the viewport and keyboard modifiers. SetEmphasis accepts one emphasis state per mesh ID. The presenter applies selection, segment-selection, sibling, dimmed and hover material policies from the selected StructuralPreviewPalette. StructuralPreviewPalette.Sgt and .Erft are the adapter presets. They differ in member color boost, surfaces, selection and hover colors, and edge and outline settings, and use the same renderer. The presenter adds a pivot marker to the supplied overlay canvas while orbiting. The marker and all generated WPF objects have their data context cleared or blocked so tool data contexts do not flow into the stable visual tree. Home views and camera movement The ExteriorThreeQuarter strategy is the SGT home view. When bounds or the exterior normal changes, the session recomputes and stores a raw Home camera. Its exact formula is: distance = max(2.2 * boundsDiagonal, 8) yaw = 28 degrees pitch = 0.22 downward along the configured up axis The exterior normal is projected onto the up plane. A missing horizontal normal uses negative Y as the stable fallback. The stored Home keeps this exact distance. Clamping applies to the displayed camera only. If the user has moved the camera, a changed scene clamps the current camera and retains the new raw Home for a later reset. Reset clears the moved flag, applies Home, and clamps the displayed camera. ERFT uses the PreserveAngle strategy. When bounds change, the session fits the current view angle and captures that result as Home. The fit formula is: halfV = radians(fieldOfView) / 2 halfH = atan(tan(halfV) * aspect) distance = max(boundsDiagonal / 2 / sin(min(halfV, halfH)), 2) * 1.2 Helix FieldOfView is the vertical angle. The fit keeps the bounds' bounding sphere inside both the vertical and the horizontal field of view, so the whole scene is visible at the viewport aspect when the fit runs; the distance clamp still applies. Scene constraints use these bounds-only constants (StructuralPreviewCameraMath): diagonal = actualDiagonal, or 10 when actualDiagonal <= 1e-6 min = clamp(diagonal * 0.0005, 0.005, 0.75) max = clamp(diagonal * 40, min * 2, 50000) targetPad = max(2, diagonal * 6) near = max(0.0005, min * 0.05) far = max(100, max * 2) When a scene changes mesh geometry without changing these bounds, the presenter keeps the stored Home object and only updates its owned render models. Adapters must compute bounds from every mesh vertex so a real extent change is reported as a bounds change; a bounds change is an intentional Home refit under PreserveAngle. ZoomToFit performs the exact fit. When FitRedefinesHome is enabled, the fitted camera becomes Home and the viewport default camera is updated to the same pose; otherwise the fit marks the camera as user-moved while preserving Home. ResetView restores stored Home. Pan uses screen-space camera axes, orbit uses the configured arbitrary up axis around the selected or picked pivot, and wheel zoom moves toward the picked world anchor. Gesture cancellation occurs on lost capture, window deactivation, unload and disabled interaction. The viewport's native view cube handles its own preview input before scene picking. The presenter keeps the default camera synchronized with stored scene Home when a scene is attached; an explicit fit also updates it when FitRedefinesHome is enabled. Input and hover StructuralPreview3DOptions.ShowTooltips defaults to true. It enables the stable presenter's mesh tooltips. When disabled, pointer updates keep the tooltip closed. Materials and lighting Adapters choose StructuralPreviewPalette.Sgt or .Erft and can copy the record to adjust individual values. A palette supplies member and context surfaces, key/fill/rim/ambient light colors, sibling and dimmed policies, selection and hover colors, emissive scaling, edge colors and thickness, outline mode and pivot colors. IsPickable controls hit testing. A non-pickable context mesh remains rendered with its base context material but bypasses selection, segment-selection, sibling, dimmed and hover emphasis; pickable context meshes can receive context hover, sibling and dimmed states but never member selection states. The SGT preset uses these alpha rules. Sibling emphasis scales diffuse alpha by 0.70 and retains the source ambient, specular and emissive alpha. Dimmed emphasis sets every channel's alpha to max(0.05, sourceAlpha * 0.45). Hovering a sibling restores the base material and adds emissive brightness while preserving its source alpha. Hovering a dimmed mesh adds emissive brightness and retains the dimmed alpha. The default options select the SGT palette and exterior home strategy. ERFT selects both its palette and its camera strategy: var options = new StructuralPreview3DOptions { Palette = StructuralPreviewPalette.Erft, HomeView = StructuralPreviewHomeView.PreserveAngle }; Diagnostics and projection Diagnostic reports debug, warning and error messages as plain strings with an optional exception. Repeated identical diagnostic messages are suppressed for two seconds. An initialization or disabled-path diagnostic is delivered once to the first diagnostic subscriber; the reason is also available in Status. Event publication takes an invocation-list snapshot and stops when a callback disposes the presenter. No presenter event is raised after Dispose clears subscriptions. On the first render failure, the presenter changes to Unavailable, disables interaction, cancels navigation, clears hover state, stops its clamp timer and collapses the viewport. It reports that failure as an error diagnostic, subject to the two-second diagnostic de-duplication; later render failures are ignored while the presenter is unavailable. TryProjectToViewport returns false when the presenter is unavailable, disposed, unloaded, has no render context, receives a non-finite point, has an invalid camera or the point is behind the camera. It returns WPF device- independent coordinates relative to the viewport on success. Projection failures are reported as debug diagnostics and never escape as exceptions. Public API The following declarations are the public API. Rendering records are in dbtools.Presentation.StructuralPreview.Rendering; configuration and events are in dbtools.Presentation.StructuralPreview. public static class StructuralPreview3DFactory { public static IStructuralPreview3D Attach( ContentControl viewportHost, Canvas? overlay, StructuralPreview3DOptions options); } public interface IStructuralPreview3D : IDisposable { bool IsAvailable { get; } StructuralPreview3DStatus Status { get; } event EventHandler? StatusChanged; event EventHandler<StructuralPreviewPointerEventArgs>? Clicked; event EventHandler<StructuralPreviewPointerEventArgs>? HoverChanged; event EventHandler<StructuralPreviewDiagnosticEventArgs>? Diagnostic; void SetScene(StructuralScene3D? scene); void SetEmphasis(StructuralEmphasis emphasis); void SetInteractive(bool active); void ResetView(); void ZoomToFit(); bool TryProjectToViewport(Vector3 world, out Point viewportPoint); } public sealed record StructuralPreview3DOptions { public Vector3 UpAxis { get; init; } = Vector3.UnitZ; public double FieldOfView { get; init; } = 45; public int Msaa { get; init; } = 4; public bool EnableSsao { get; init; } = true; public bool ShowViewCube { get; init; } = true; public bool ShowTooltips { get; init; } = true; public StructuralPreviewHomeView HomeView { get; init; } = StructuralPreviewHomeView.ExteriorThreeQuarter; public bool FitRedefinesHome { get; init; } public StructuralPreviewPalette Palette { get; init; } = StructuralPreviewPalette.Sgt; } public enum StructuralPreviewHomeView { ExteriorThreeQuarter, PreserveAngle } public sealed record StructuralPreview3DStatus( StructuralPreview3DState State, string? Reason = null); public enum StructuralPreview3DState { Ready, Unavailable, Disposed } public enum StructuralPreviewDiagnosticLevel { Debug, Warning, Error } public sealed class StructuralPreviewDiagnosticEventArgs( StructuralPreviewDiagnosticLevel level, string message, Exception? exception = null) : EventArgs { public StructuralPreviewDiagnosticLevel Level { get; } = level; public string Message { get; } = message; public Exception? Exception { get; } = exception; } public sealed class StructuralPreviewPointerEventArgs( string? meshId, string? contextId, Point screenPoint, Vector3? worldPoint, ModifierKeys modifiers) : EventArgs { public string? MeshId { get; } = meshId; public string? ContextId { get; } = contextId; public Point ScreenPoint { get; } = screenPoint; public Vector3? WorldPoint { get; } = worldPoint; public ModifierKeys Modifiers { get; } = modifiers; } public enum StructuralPreviewOutlineMode { CreaseEdges, AllEdges } public sealed record StructuralPreviewSurface( Vector3 Ambient, Vector3 Specular, float EmissiveFactor, float Shininess = 30); The palette declaration exposes the following complete public surface: public sealed record StructuralPreviewPalette { public static StructuralPreviewPalette Sgt { get; } public static StructuralPreviewPalette Erft { get; } public float MemberColorBoost { get; init; } = 0.18f; public uint BackgroundArgb { get; init; } = 0xFF1E1E28; public Vector4 KeyLightColor { get; init; } = Vector4.One; public Vector4 FillLightColor { get; developer-guide/architecture/test-pipeli.title: Test Pipeline | dbtools
developer-guide/architecture/test-pipeli.summary: Test Pipeline This page describes how dbtools tests are selected, staged and run. For the test.sh options, examples and the rules for writing tests, see Testing Tools. dbtools tests run through one of two routes: ./test.sh resolves the selected projects, builds them, freezes their inputs and runs them locally or submits them to the dbtools-daemon fleet. It writes the receipts that --no-build and CI consume. See the test.sh command reference. Plain dotnet test on an entry project in testing/Daemon/ uses the pinned daemon VSTest adapter (dbtools-daemon.RevitTest.TestAdapter). MSBuild builds the selected assemblies, models, includes and per-year sources, and the adapter submits them in one request. See Daemon adapter entry projects. Use one route per invocation. Both read the relay URL from DBTOOLS_DAEMON_RELAY_URL; the daemon owns relay credentials, and neither route accepts or stores them. Scopes and suites Scope or suite Marker Where it runs Pure tests (pure) plain [Test] Without Revit. Locally when possible; otherwise as a daemon PureSuite job on a hidden Windows desktop Revit-hosted tests (local) [RevitLocal] Inside Revit on a daemon worker, for one selected year Design Automation tests (da) [RevitDA] On the invoking host as a budgeted APS client; external run records feed Studio DIST The Windows distribution acceptance suite, always a daemon PureSuite job BUILD Linux-native build and distribution contract suites Revit-hosted tests exercise the real ribbon, WPF and add-in lifecycle in Revit. The scheduled runner builds the Revit 2026 Sentinel test project and submits one capped WorkItem. Offline Sentinel tests use the Pure scope. See APS Design Automation Sentinel. Pure requests have no year. A Revit-hosted request for two years makes one daemon request per year, each with its own product tree and report. Design Automation tests always build Revit 2026. Selection test.sh list --projects prints the sorted scope<TAB>project rows and is the source of truth for what a request selects. It evaluates project membership, explicit Compile Include, Exclude and Remove items, disabled default items, NUnit fixture attributes and the selected tool, scope and year. The same index resolves fixtures and exact FQNs. A fixture must resolve to one compiled owner class. An unknown fixture or project, an unreadable project or source file, a project the selected tool and scope cannot reach, or an explicit scope with no resolved project exits with status 2 before any build or submission. An exact FullyQualifiedName=<FQN> filter becomes an exact daemon selector, and a prefix filter becomes a prefix selector. A Revit-hosted filter that cannot be mapped exits with status 2 instead of selecting the whole assembly. Pure routing test.sh checks each selected Pure assembly for its .deps.json, .runtimeconfig.json and the output-local NUnit3.TestAdapter.dll, then routes it: to the daemon if it is the DIST suite or a machine is pinned; to the daemon if it targets Windows and the host is not Windows; to the daemon if the host lacks Microsoft.WindowsDesktop.App; a missing other framework is an error; otherwise to local VSTest. Projects that run locally, including the Linux BUILD and Distribution suites, run one after another; daemon submissions run concurrently, at most DBT_PURE_CONCURRENCY (default 2) at a time. A local project that runs zero tests fails. With a filter expression, the run fails only when no selected project runs a test. Linux-native BUILD projects and *.Portable.Pure.Tests projects are skipped on Windows with a notice. User interface input By default, a daemon job, Pure or Revit-hosted, runs on the daemon's private desktop, which receives no keyboard or mouse input and never becomes the foreground, whether the Windows session is locked or not. Tests drive the user interface in-process: through view-model commands, WPF automation peer providers, RaiseEvent, Keyboard.Focus or FocusManager in the test's own windows, and the calling thread's own Win32 state (SetActiveWindow, SetKeyboardState, messages to its own windows); or through UI Automation patterns in another process. A test project fails to build when it uses an API listed in testing/BannedSymbols.txt (error RS0030) or when its source names an OS input or foreground function such as SendInput or SetForegroundWindow (error DBT0003, DBT_RejectOsInputInterop in Directory.Build.targets). Inputs and receipts For a selected scope and year, the MSBuild graph returns the test assembly, target framework, model items and product-tree includes in one pass. Before any submission, test.sh freezes the assemblies, runtime closure, product-tree includes, models and companions into the content-addressed test input cache (DBT_TEST_INPUT_CACHE_ROOT), so a later build cannot change the submitted files. A normal exit removes the per-run directory. The default cache is $TMPDIR/dbtools-test-inputs/<repository hash>; with it, each test and submit deletes the caches of other repositories in that folder that no run used for 7 days. --compile-only writes a receipt bound to the source identity, the selected projects, the graph inputs and the output hashes. The source identity hashes HEAD, the output of git diff HEAD, and untracked files that Git does not ignore. It hashes the same inputs for each untracked Git checkout. --no-build verifies the receipt and refuses stale or missing files. CI resolves the selectors once with ./test.sh list --projects, compiles each selected scope with --compile-only, transfers the receipt and the recorded input closure, and runs them with --no-build. The consumer never rebuilds. Linux BUILD and DIST jobs do not depend on the Windows transfer. The portable BUILD project selection requires no prebuilt product or candidate output: ./test.sh test --tool BUILD --project testing/dbtools.Build.Tests/dbtools.Build.Tests.csproj --scope pure --filter 'TestCategory!=ProductArtifacts' --tool BUILD also selects the Distribution and Sandbox projects. Their setup requirements remain separate. Ordinary test compilation creates test artifacts under .artifacts. On Linux, dbtools.Distribution.Tests restores and builds Sandbox for each supported Revit year when the test project compiles. The Sandbox owner cases load these builds and resolve window owners from the Release distribution produced by BuildAll. The complete --filter 'TestCategory=ProductArtifacts' selection requires a source-current ./build.sh BuildAll and compiled hosted test outputs. It checks promoted distributions, compiler PDBs, merge inputs and hosted test outputs. AssembleDistributionCandidate alone does not supply all of these inputs. Artifact admission inspects every staged build.json and the final record. It selects the newest parsed builtAtUtc whose sourceCommit and sourceTree match HEAD and its tree. Admission requires clean tracked and untracked source, including root build configuration and documentation. Distributed bytes must match the declared distributionFingerprint before tests read them. Compiler PDBs, merge inputs and dependency files require current BuildAll outputs as setup; the distribution fingerprint does not authenticate those intermediate files. The Presentation ToolWindowXamlTests fixture, compiled by Presentation Pure, parses raw XAML from every tool in DistributionContract.ToolAssemblyFiles and Core. Its project references supply the complete tool set to the test consumer. Results Daemon summary and full-report JSON require a command envelope with the report under result.report. A document without the envelope fails validation. After a zero submit exit, the summary must report result_status=passed, a positive passed count, and zero failed, errored, and aborted counts. Skipped tests can accompany passed tests. Zero executed tests, including an all-skipped run, fail admission. A nonzero submit exit is kept even when the terminal JSON is missing or malformed. When retrieval succeeds, failed runs keep their reports and original exit status. A refused submit (ok: false, a null result and an error) ran nothing: the wrapper prints the error code, summary, causes and next step, fetches no report, and keeps the CLI's nonzero exit, or returns 2 after a zero exit. Other rejected terminal summaries are saved as *.invalid-summary.json. Full report retrieval accepts a report exit of zero or the submit exit. The report file must be nonempty, and its JSON request identity, status, and counts must match the accepted summary. Retrieval makes three report attempts, stopping after the first accepted report. Two one-second delays separate three failed attempts. It never resubmits tests. Only an accepted report is published to the result path. After exhaustion, nonempty rejected output is saved as PATH.invalid-report.json, where PATH is the full report path. A refused report command prints its error code, summary, causes and next step whatever its exit; only a refusal with exit 3 is fetched again, and a refused report is not saved. The wrapper keeps a nonzero submit exit or returns 2 after a zero submit exit. Independent scopes in one request continue after a failure, but test.sh returns the first nonzero status. Daemon adapter entry projects testing/Daemon/Hosted/<Tool>.Hosted.Entry.csproj builds dbtools.<Tool>.Local.Tests for both years (Hosted2026.proj, Hosted2027.proj). <Tool> is a tool key or App, Core or Presentation. The App, Core and GM entries also build dbtools.<Tool>.HostedTurns.Local.Tests. testing/Daemon/Pure/<Tool>.Pure.Entry.csproj selects every dbtools.<Tool>.*Pure.Tests.csproj beside its owner. After the build, the entry writes dbtools-daemon.runsettings from Hosted.runsettings or Pure.runsettings with the literal sources, models and includes. The hosted settings default to years 2026,2027, isolated execution and a 30-minute timeout, and treat a run with no tests as an error. Product staging Each Revit-hosted test for a year receives the product tree that the installer uses, under product/<year>/. The tree keeps its relative paths. Test assemblies and NUnit and adapter dependencies are separate inputs. App loads tools from Tools/ by explicit path into the context that holds it, so ProductLoadContext and DevModeLoadContext receive the same identities as the staged tree. Test support installs no resolver for product assemblies. Test projects Test projects are next to their production owners: src/dbtools.App/Tests/dbtools.App.{Pure,Local}.Tests.csproj src/dbtools.Core/Tests/dbtools.Core.{Pure,Local}.Tests.csproj src/dbtools.Presentation/Tests/dbtools.Presentation.{Pure,Local}.Tests.csproj src/dbtools.Sandbox/Tests/dbtools.Sandbox.Pure.Tests.csproj src/Tools/<Category>/<Tool>/Tests/dbtools.<Tool>.{Pure,Local}.Tests.csproj testing/dbtools.Build.Tests/ build and distribution contracts (Linux) testing/dbtools.Distribution.Tests/ portable archive contracts, Dev Mode unload (Linux) testing/dbtools.Distribution.Windows.Tests/ DIST suite testing/RevitTestModels/ test models by year and tool An owner has both a .Pure.Tests and a .Local.Tests project only when both kinds of test exist. Pure projects list their source files explicitly and reference their normal production owners. Shared props give every Pure project $(DBT_PureRevitYear) (2026) and static graph restore, and pass that year on owner references, so a plain dotnet build or dotnet test of one project needs no properties. Windows Pure projects compile against the pinned desktop Revit references. Their runtime output contains IL-only copies of RevitAPI, RevitAPIUI, AdWindows, and UIFramework. These stubs preserve Revit type definitions, constants, and enum values. A stub method throws NotSupportedException with the message <assembly> is a test stub. Its API calls require the host. This applies during type initialization and when GetCustomAttribute<TransactionAttribute>() constructs a Revit attribute. An NUnit action records the exception when it is thrown and fails the case even if a catch block handles it. Mark a test with [AllowRevitStubCalls] when it checks the stub failure itself. Sandbox Pure leaves assembly resolution to the Sandbox Revit runtime resolver. .Local.Tests projects disable default compile items and include only Revit-hosted fixtures. Presentation tests are under Presentation and belong to the Presentation projects, also when they test a tool's Presentation types. Presentation Pure links the Core test support it shares and references Core for the tool window, window runtime and logger window integration fixtures. Tests that need a real WPF window run where Windows is available. Portable Pure projects Core and the Super Girt Tool (SGT) define an optional $(DBT_PortableTargetFramework). Their *.Portable.Pure.Tests projects build against that framework and run on Linux; CI and Windows test.sh route them to Linux. To make a project portable: declare desktop and portable TargetFrameworks; condition DBT_RevitHostIdentity, UseWPF and the Presentation ProjectReference on the desktop framework, and keep Revit references under the desktop host identity condition; set DBT_UsesMergedAssemblies=false in portable consumers. build/MSBuild/Portable.targets excludes App, Revit, Views, DesignTime and XAML inputs. Portable images use ordinary NuGet dependencies, have no content version and add no staged runtime files. Core uses an explicit list of source files for its portable build. Test models Revit-hosted projects declare RevitTestModel items relative to testing/RevitTestModels: testing/RevitTestModels/ ├── 2026/GM/gm_test_model.rvt ├── 2026/SGT/sgt_test_model.rvt ├── 2026/SGT/_LinkedModels/sgt_test_linked_model.rvt ├── 2026/Regression/realtest_model.rvt ├── 2027/... (same layout) ├── GM/SharedParameters/shared_parameters.txt └── VTC/vtc_import_layers.dxf Model files and explicit non-RVT inputs keep their relative paths in the daemon stage. Revit-hosted fixtures find them under DBTOOLS_DAEMON_REVIT_MODELS_DIR; Pure fixtures use the repository root in DBT_TEST_REPO_ROOT. TestPathResolver reads the root on every call, so a job never sees the model root of a previous job. A fixture may open a temporary copy of a model, but the daemon owns the active document and the worker lifecycle. Models resolve only from these roots, not from a worker checkout or an %APPDATA% cache. Test support testing/TestSupport holds shared test infrastructure and doubles for true externals. Tool-specific doubles are under testing/TestSupport/<Tool> and are linked as source by the matching test projects; they are not a separate assembly. Revit/RevitHost.cs starts the App lifecycle and opens an explicit API scope with the UIApplication for the synchronous prefix of the test body. The scope closes when the body returns its task. Hosted tool fixtures borrow the App service root's task, which also serves App QueuedModeless run scopes. A fixture that constructs its own Revit task owns its disposal. Hosted startup advances queued hook attachment through the real event handler and completes deferred UI startup. While no Revit calls are pending, AppHostedComposition advances the dispatcher with a bounded Background operation. The startup wait preserves the caller's API scope and leaves input to WPF. One daemon callback has no second native Revit turn. A forced-queue test can call the real event handler synchronously to exercise queue dispatch. Use a RevitHostedTurns fixture to test work across native turns. RevitCallGateModelessHostedTurnCertificationTests uses it to verify that Revit delivers work queued during a progress frame in a later native turn. Wpf/WpfTestRuntimeBootstrap.cs registers pack URI support, installs the shared window owner, validates themes in the runtime assembly's contextual reflection scope, and releases only its own provider at teardown. It adds no Resolving handlers and does not force Presentation into the default context. Logging/TestLoggingBridge.cs uses production logging when Revit provides it and a console and file host otherwise. Each opted-in test assembly uses one App lifecycle, one Revit task and one main-window owner. Assembly teardown shuts them down before the next assembly starts in the same Revit process. A hosted WindowStaticRuntimeTestScope releases its window configuration and retires dispatcher work at teardown. Profile setup disables view-activated model updates for Elevation Tags, Combined Foundation Tags and Joist Girder Weights. The production hooks attach. A fixture that tests automatic updates enables its tool through the settings provider. Fixtures release their windows, document leases and other owned resources. The shared after-test action checks the App registry for retained tool windows. Cleanup reports both the primary failure and any cleanup failure. See Build Pipeline, Assembly Loading Contract and Sandbox Validator.

developer-guide/architecture/theme-syste.title: Theme System | dbtools
developer-guide/architecture/theme-syste.summary: Theme System dbtools.Presentation.dll holds the compiled WPF resources that must stay loaded for the life of the Revit process: theme dictionaries, stable controls and window shells, and settings views that register WPF dependency properties. Other tool views are raw XAML that Presentation parses at run time, so App, Core and tool assemblies contain no BAML or .g.resources. Each window merges the theme into its own resources, never into Application.Resources, so dbtools does not change the appearance of other add-ins. Assembly roles Assembly Compiled WPF content dbtools.Presentation Theme dictionaries, stable windows, controls, tool behaviors, converters, ElevationTags and FoundationTags settings views, and the merged Helix theme dbtools.Core None. Window lifecycle, error boundaries, registry, commands and runtime hosts can be reloaded Tool assemblies None. Tool views and markup-only settings views are embedded as raw XAML Presentation lists its Page and EmbeddedResource items explicitly (EnableDefaultPageItems=false); default Compile inclusion picks up their code-behind. Tool assemblies contain no compiled WPF pages. A compiled settings view lives in Presentation under Tools/<TOOL>/, in namespace dbtools.Presentation.Tools.<TOOL>, when its code-behind registers WPF dependency properties. ElevationTags and FoundationTags use this form. DialogSuppression and JoistGirderWeight embed markup-only settings views in their tool assemblies as raw XAML. Settings pack views AddDbtSettingsPackDefinition<TOptions, TContext> accepts a view factory with the type Func<ISettingsPackContext<TOptions>, FrameworkElement>. A tool module supplies the view in one of two forms: a compiled view from dbtools.Presentation.Tools.<TOOL>, created with new and given the context as DataContext; a markup-only view embedded in the tool as raw XAML with the logical name dbtools.ToolViews.<TOOL>.<View>.xaml, which the factory loads with ToolWindowXaml.LoadElement before it assigns the DataContext. TDV's LibrarySettingsView uses this form through TdvToolModule.LoadLibrarySettingsView. A view that registers dependency properties or needs code-behind uses the compiled form. Tool views A tool embeds each view as an EmbeddedResource with the logical name dbtools.ToolViews.<TOOL>.<View>.xaml. ToolWindowFactory.CreateModal or CreateModeless (Core) opens a view in a stable shell. The modal factory returns IModalToolWindowSession with ShowDialog and HideForPick. The modeless factory returns IModelessToolWindowSession with Show. Both inherit the common lifecycle surface from IToolWindowSession. Creation runs these steps: ToolWindowHost.CreateModal or CreateModeless (Presentation) creates a stable shell, ToolWindowModalShell or ToolWindowModelessShell. The shell initializer runs before the view is parsed. The default is WindowInitializer.Initialize or InitializeModeless, which applies the theme, binds the owner window, registers the progress overlay and installs the error boundary and logging. ToolWindowXaml.LoadElement parses the raw view inside ToolWindowReflectionScope, and the view and shell receive the tool's view model as DataContext. The factory registers the session in ToolWindowRegistry. The caller shows the window with session.ShowDialog() or session.Show() and gets named controls with session.Require<T>(name). The Settings, Alert, Logger and notification banner windows are raw resources in Presentation and use the same loader; so do tool template dictionaries such as the View Template Comparer (VTC) diff templates and the Super Girt Tool (SGT) opening view. For these windows Core keeps the state, commands and lifecycle and event handling; the controls need no typed constructor from a reloadable assembly and do no type discovery at run time. Retirement tears down bindings, automation roots, resources and callbacks. Core lifecycle handlers are released through BehaviorState and session cleanup before the shell closes. A custom shell initializer releases its own handles. Raw views name only framework types or public stable Presentation types and merge the theme through Presentation's ResourceUri markup extension before they use static theme keys. Tool content uses explicit keyed templates. SGT's opening and girt grids use stable behaviors over tool row state. The Extreme Roof Framing Tool (ERFT) and SGT pass immutable scene data to the stable 3D viewport, which owns camera, material, picking and device state (see Structural Preview). Theme dictionaries The root dictionary is: /dbtools.Presentation;V<PresentationVersion>;component/Resources/Theme.xaml <PresentationVersion> is the content version of the Presentation assembly (see Build Pipeline).
