The root merges, in this order: /dbtools.Presentation;V<PresentationVersion>;component/Resources/Tokens.xaml /dbtools.Presentation;V<PresentationVersion>;component/Resources/Brushes.Dark.xaml or Brushes.Light.xaml, the brushes of the current color theme /dbtools.Presentation;V<PresentationVersion>;component/Resources/Converters.xaml /dbtools.Presentation;V<PresentationVersion>;component/Resources/Controls.xaml /dbtools.Presentation;V<PresentationVersion>;component/Resources/DataGrid.xaml /dbtools.Presentation;V<PresentationVersion>;component/Resources/Menus.xaml /dbtools.Presentation;V<PresentationVersion>;component/Resources/Components.xaml The theme uses plain WPF controls and no control library. Each implicit style that changes the look of a control supplies the control's whole template, so no WPF system theme template draws a dbtools control. A style that extends another dbtools style uses BasedOn only within the same dictionary file: when WPF loads a dictionary from its Source, a StaticResource in that file sees only the file, the dictionaries that the file merges itself and the system theme, not the other dictionaries that Theme.xaml merges. {StaticResource {x:Type Button}} in Components.xaml, for example, finds the system theme's Button style. Across files, a style or template uses DynamicResource; the TreeView style of VTC sets Template to {DynamicResource TreeViewTemplate} from Controls.xaml. ThemeResourceLoader (Core) checks this order. At startup ThemeValidator.ValidateOrThrow registers the pack URI scheme, loads each dictionary separately for both color themes and freezes its freezables, loads the root and checks its merged dictionaries, and then measures and arranges a probe tree of standard controls. A failure stops startup; see Troubleshooting. Color themes dbtools has two color themes, Dark and Light. One theme applies to every dbtools window. The user chooses it under General > Appearance in Settings. The initial theme follows the Revit UI theme that UIThemeManager.CurrentTheme reports at startup. ColorThemeState (Presentation) holds Current and Default. At startup AppStartupPreparationWorkflow sets Default from the Revit UI theme and starts ColorThemeSettingsObserver (Core) with the saved SettingsFlags.Theme. The observer applies the theme again on each published flag change, so a change in the Settings window shows at once; Save keeps it. Theme.xaml merges the brush dictionary of Current through {dbtResources:ThemeBrushesUri}: Resources/Brushes.Dark.xaml or Resources/Brushes.Light.xaml. Both define the same keys. ColorThemeState.Apply reloads every loaded brush dictionary, and open windows take the new brushes through their DynamicResource references. It runs on the Revit UI thread, which every dbtools window shares; a brush dictionary of another UI thread keeps its brushes. A brush that code reads once with FindResource keeps its old value until the code reads it again. ThemeValidator loads both brush dictionaries at startup, so a broken dictionary stops startup and not a later theme switch. Brush roles ThemeBrushKeys names semantic roles. New XAML uses them: Role Use SurfaceWindow, SurfaceCard, SurfaceControl Elevation: window, card or panel, control rest fill. Each step is lighter in Dark SurfaceWell, SurfaceOverlay A list or grid inset in a card; popups, menus and tooltips FillHover, FillPressed Opaque hover and pressed fills of controls FillSubtleHover, FillSubtlePressed Translucent overlays for rows, tabs and borderless buttons FillSelected, FillSelectedHover, FillDisabled Selection and disabled filled buttons StrokeDivider, StrokeControl, StrokeField, StrokeFocus, StrokeWindow, StrokeDisabled Hairlines, button borders, field borders (3:1), the gold focus ring, window edges Text, TextSecondary, TextMuted, TextDisabled, TextPlaceholder Text levels; disabled text stays readable (4.5:1) TextAccent, TextSelected, TextSelectedSecondary, TextDanger, TextAttention Blue text, text on a selected row, error text, the Modified marker AccentFill*, DangerFill*, Attention Primary and danger buttons, the attention dot Banner* Notification banner surface, outline, kind colors and tints The older hue- and feature-named keys (Paper, Surface, Body, ButtonPrimary and the others) remain for existing XAML. Where a role has the same meaning, the older key holds the role's value. Tokens Tokens.xaml holds the compact density and the ramps: Density: Size.Control and Size.Row are the compact 28 px control and row height; MinHeight.Button, MinHeight.Control and Size.DataGridRow.MinHeight equal them. Size.ControlSmall (24 px) is for header actions. Type: FontFamily.UI (Segoe UI) and FontFamily.Icon; sizes 12, 13, 15 and 20 (FontSize.Caption, FontSize.Body, FontSize.Subtitle and FontSize.Title, FontSize.Header), with LineHeight.*. WindowThemeApplicator sets each window's font to FontFamily.UI and FontSize.Body, so text does not follow the system message font. Spacing: the 4 px ramp Spacing4 to Spacing32, and role insets and gaps (Inset.Button, Inset.Input, Inset.Row, Inset.Card, Inset.Dialog, Inset.Footer, Gap.Stack, Gap.Section, Gap.Label). Radius: Radius4 for controls, Radius8 for cards and dialogs. Shared controls dbtools.Presentation.Controls holds the controls that views share. Raw views reach them with xmlns:controls="clr-namespace:dbtools.Presentation.Controls;assembly=dbtools.Presentation". Their styles are in the theme. Control Use DialogFooter The buttons at the bottom of a dialog. The theme sets each action button's Height to Size.Control (28 device-independent pixels). DialogFooter.Role places each child: Tertiary at the left (Reset All, Copy details), then at the right Secondary (Cancel, Validate) and the one Primary, which is rightmost whatever the declaration order. The tab order follows. In a destructive confirmation the danger button takes Primary and Cancel sets IsDefault, so Enter cancels SearchBox A filter text box with a magnifier, a Placeholder that names what it filters, an optional ResultText such as 2 of 12 and a clear button while there is text. Escape clears; the clear button and Escape update the Text binding at once. It is a TextBox, so its Text binding and automation id work as before SettingsPack A flat card with a Title. IsModified shows Modified and enables Reset to defaults, which runs ResetCommand. HasPendingChanges shows Unsaved independently. UI Automation sees a group and ResetAutomationId names the button. ToolbarRow Commands that act on the list or content next to them, left to right with an 8 px gap ListEmptyState.Text An attached property: the line that a ListBox, TreeView or DataGrid shows while it has no items AlertWindowViewModel orders the alert footer the same way: secondary and Cancel buttons, then the primary button, then a danger button at the right. An alert with a danger button makes its Cancel button the default. Every window that WindowInitializer sets up gets a title bar in the colors of the color theme (WindowCaption): dark or light caption, the SurfaceWindow caption fill, Text caption text and the StrokeWindow border. On Windows 10 the window keeps the system caption. A theme change repaints open windows. Control behaviors The theme sets two behaviors on standard controls: Nested scrolling. The implicit ScrollViewer style sets WheelForwarding.IsEnabled. A scroll viewer that cannot move in the direction of a wheel turn passes the turn to the scroll viewer around it. This covers the viewers in the templates of TextBox, ListBox, ListView and TreeView, so a short list, tree or text box inside a scrolling page does not stop the page. DataGridMouseWheelBehavior does the same for a grid at the end of its range. A viewer in a popup keeps its wheel. A ScrollViewer with its own keyed style gets the behavior only if that style is based on the implicit one. Long text in grids. DataGridTextCell cuts long text with an ellipsis. While the text is cut, CutTextToolTip shows the whole text in the tool tip; a tool tip that the cell sets itself stays. DataGridColumnsBehavior gives generated text columns this style. A declared column sets ElementStyle="{StaticResource DataGridTextCell}": a grid column is not in the element tree, so a DynamicResource on a column property finds only application resources and the cell keeps the default style. DataGridTextCell.Wrap wraps a message column; give that column Width="*", so rows grow and the grid does not scroll sideways. Resource URIs Every compiled resource URI contains the assembly's version. A changed stable assembly therefore has a new identity, and WPF cannot select an older copy of Presentation that an earlier dbtools version has already loaded. The component URI is relative, so Application.LoadComponent does not need the pack scheme to be registered. Use ResourceUri.CreateResourceUri for Application.LoadComponent, dictionary sources and the dictionary markup extensions. Use ResourceUri.CreateAbsoluteResourceUri for images and icons created in code without a WPF base URI. It registers the pack scheme and returns pack://application:,,,/<assembly>;V<version>;component/<path>. WindowInitializer loads the window icon with BitmapCacheOption.OnLoad inside its warning boundary; otherwise WPF can defer the file lookup until it creates the window handle. XAML namespaces XAML outside Presentation refers to stable types with clr-namespace:...;assembly=dbtools.Presentation. XAML compiled by Presentation uses the namespace form without assembly=. This keeps the BAML compiler from resolving Presentation types through a reloadable assembly. BAML assembly versions The BAML assembly table must contain the final assembly version, because WPF resolves local markup extensions through that table separately from the outer pack URI. Keep SDK assembly-info generation on in WPF temporary projects. With it off, BAML references Version=0.0.0.0; if an older Presentation is already loaded in the default context, the CLR can satisfy that request with the older copy. When that copy lacks a markup extension type that the current BAML names, WPF throws NotImplementedException before it opens the merged dictionaries. WPF's local-assembly fallback runs only when loading throws, so a successful bind to the older copy bypasses it. See .NET 10 WPF assembly and type resolution and CoreCLR version compatibility. Source files File Responsibility src/dbtools.Presentation/dbtools.Presentation.csproj Assembly identity and the explicit list of compiled pages and embedded views src/dbtools.Presentation/Resources/Theme.xaml Root theme dictionary src/dbtools.Presentation/Resources/Brushes.Dark.xaml, Brushes.Light.xaml The brushes of each color theme, with the same keys src/dbtools.Presentation/Theming/ColorThemeState.cs The current and default color theme; reloads open brush dictionaries src/dbtools.Core/UI/Theming/ColorThemeSettingsObserver.cs Applies SettingsFlags.Theme at startup and on each flag change src/dbtools.Presentation/Controls/ Shared controls src/dbtools.Presentation/Windows/WindowCaption.cs Title bar colors src/dbtools.Presentation/Behaviors/WheelForwarding.cs Wheel turns that a nested scroll viewer cannot use src/dbtools.Presentation/DataGrid/Behaviors/CutTextToolTip.cs The tool tip of cut cell text src/dbtools.Presentation/Resources/ResourceUri.cs Versioned resource URIs src/dbtools.Core/UI/Theming/ThemeResource/ThemeResourceLoader.cs Merge order check src/dbtools.Core/UI/Theming/ThemeValidator.cs Startup theme validation src/dbtools.App/dbtools.App.csproj App resources and embedded manifests; no tool XAML build/Distribution/DistributionContract.cs The product file list See dbtools.Presentation, Architecture Overview and Assembly Loading Contract.

developer-guide/architecture/wiki-server.title: Wiki Server | dbtools
developer-guide/architecture/wiki-server.summary: Wiki Server wiki/server-config/ holds the configuration of the web server that serves this documentation site at https://dbtools.greatwhitelab.net. The server runs Caddy for the static files and a webhook container that updates them. A push to the main branch of the kirsch33/dbtools-wiki repository makes the server pull the new site. Publishing flow The documentation build (.github/scripts/build-docs.sh) writes wiki/_site. Publishing pushes the site to the main branch of kirsch33/dbtools-wiki. GitHub sends the push event of kirsch33/dbtools-wiki to https://dbtools.greatwhitelab.net/hooks/dbtools-wiki, signed with the shared secret in the X-Hub-Signature-256 header. Caddy proxies /hooks/* to the webhook container on port 9000. The dbtools-wiki hook runs only when the HMAC-SHA256 signature is valid, repository.full_name is kirsch33/dbtools-wiki and ref is refs/heads/main. It then runs /scripts/pull-site.sh dbtools-wiki. pull-site.sh reads the site entry from sites.json. On first use it clones the branch with depth 1 into the web directory; after that it fetches the branch and runs git reset --hard origin/<branch>. Caddy serves /web/dbtools-wiki as static files. A path that matches no file or directory returns /index.html. Files File Content Dockerfile The webhook image: almir/webhook, pinned by digest, plus bash, git and jq. It runs as the base image's unprivileged webhook user. docker-compose.yml The webhook service: builds the image, runs webhook -verbose -template -hooks=/etc/webhook/hooks.json -hotreload, mounts config/ and scripts/ read-only and /web read-write, reads webhook.env, and joins the external caddy_default network. webhook.env.example Template for webhook.env, which sets WEBHOOK_SECRET. config/hooks.json The hook definitions. -template lets each hook read WEBHOOK_SECRET with getenv. config/sites.json Maps a site name to repo (GitHub owner/name), web_dir and branch (default main). scripts/pull-site.sh pull-site.sh <site-name>: clones or updates one site from sites.json. It exits with status 1 when the name is missing or unknown, or sites.json is absent. caddy-snippet.txt The Caddy site block for dbtools.greatwhitelab.net. hooks.json and sites.json also define a blog site (kirsch33/blog, served from /web/blog) that uses the same script. Requirements Docker with Compose, and a Caddy container on the external Docker network caddy_default. The image needs bash, git and jq, because pull-site.sh uses all three. The base image has only the webhook binary and /bin/sh; the Dockerfile adds them with apk. The host directory /web must be writable by the UID:GID in the user field of docker-compose.yml (1001:1001). Set it to the server user that owns the bind mounts. The site repository must be readable over anonymous HTTPS, because pull-site.sh clones https://github.com/<repo>.git without credentials. The GitHub webhook and webhook.env must use the same secret. Setup Copy webhook.env.example to webhook.env and set WEBHOOK_SECRET, for example from openssl rand -hex 32. Check and start the service: docker compose config --quiet docker compose up -d --build Add the block from caddy-snippet.txt to the Caddyfile and reload Caddy. On kirsch33/dbtools-wiki, add a webhook for push events with the payload URL https://dbtools.greatwhitelab.net/hooks/dbtools-wiki, the content type application/json and the same secret. -hotreload makes the webhook reload hooks.json when the file changes. A change to the Dockerfile needs docker compose up -d --build. To move to another base image, resolve its digest and rebuild on the wiki host.

developer-guide/developing/feature-warni.title: Feature Warnings | dbtools
developer-guide/developing/feature-warni.summary: Feature Warnings A feature warning reports an actionable configuration or prerequisite problem. Active warnings block the commands named by their definitions and publish ribbon enablement updates. Warning state lasts for the current runtime session. It is not persisted to settings. The Settings window displays warning cards and opens each panel that contains an active warning. The Settings button shows a warning icon, and the dbtools tab receives a highlight when warnings exist. A disabled command's tooltip names every active warning that blocks it. Command preflight and contextual edit flows use the same registered warning policy as ribbon controls. Defining warnings in manifest.yml Declare warnings under a settings pack: tool: settingsPacks: - key: structural.foundation_tags title: "Combined Foundation Tags" warnings: - id: core.structural.combined_tags title: "Combined Foundation Tags Disabled" message: "Use Settings -> Combined Foundation Tags -> Install/Repair. A successful repair clears the warning and re-enables the commands." disableTools: - dbtools.UpdateCombinedFoundationTags - dbtools.MoveCombinedFoundationTags - dbtools.OrganizeFoundationTypes Property Requirement and meaning id Required globally unique warning identity. title Required warning-card title. message Required description and corrective action. disableTools Optional list of registered ribbon internalName values. Use stable IDs such as core.library.invalid, core.common.elevation_tags, and core.structural.joist_girder. List only commands that depend on the prerequisite. Name the problem, the affected operation, and the correction in the warning message. ToolWarningManifest carries the ID, title, message, and disabled-tool list. The manifest is metadata. It does not activate the warning by itself. Registering warning definitions Register a warning through AddDbtSettingsPackDefinition in ToolModule.RegisterSettingsPacks. The extension reads the single pack and its warning from the manifest. Settings Packs contains the full registration and the typed settings section setup. services.AddDbtSettingsPackDefinition<MyToolSettings, SettingsPackContext>( manifest, (_, input) => new SettingsPackContext(input.RequireWarningId()), context => new MyToolSettingsView { DataContext = context }, context => context.HasWarning, (context, active) => context.HasWarning = active); The extension requires exactly one warning when both flag delegates are present. It requires no warnings when both delegates are absent. The runtime warning retains the context created by its pack. Callers cannot supply another context to its getter or setter. The context owns HasWarning for presentation and editing. The settings DTO owns persisted preferences such as AutoUpdateEnabled. IAutoUpdateSettings requires only that preference. Do not serialize a warning flag or derive command blocking from a saved flag. Triggering warnings Tools use dbtools.Core.Settings.Warnings.ISettingsWarningService: IReadOnlyCollection<ISettingsWarningDefinition> Definitions { get; } bool IsWarningActive(string warningId); SettingsWarningStateChange SetWarning(string warningId, bool active); warnings.SetWarning("core.structural.combined_tags", true); if (warnings.IsWarningActive("core.structural.combined_tags")) return; Blank or unknown IDs fail. Definitions must exist in the validated settings catalog before a tool uses them. Warning lookup is ordinal and case-sensitive. SetWarning updates session state and publishes the warning and aggregate visual state. SettingsWarningStateChange reports the prior and current state. The concrete SettingsWarningService owns active-ID enumeration and replay. SettingsWarningPublicationPolicy publishes individual warning changes, full replay, and aggregate HasWarnings. Tools receive the narrowed public interface, not internal publication operations. Validation and activation A warning-aware editor implements ISettingsWarningContext.WarningId and returns an invalid SettingsValidationResult for a configuration problem. The ID must belong to that pack. Use the actual result API: public Task<SettingsValidationResult> ValidateAsync(CancellationToken ct = default) { ct.ThrowIfCancellationRequested(); return Task.FromResult(string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(LibraryPath) ? SettingsValidationResult.FromErrors("Select a library path.") : SettingsValidationResult.Success); } This excerpt checks an editor-owned LibraryPath. A real library validator must also check its required file/directory conditions. Conditional features can return Success when disabled if their configuration is unnecessary then. Do not report an unexpected I/O or programming exception as invalid settings. Validation has distinct publication rules: Operation Warning behavior Startup Load saved options into fresh runtimes without views. Activate invalid warning-aware packs. Do not proactively clear warnings. Open Settings Validate loaded options and publish warning state. A cleared warning also releases the per-document failure gate for tasks that declare it. Validate button Evaluate every pack, report its validation errors and name active warnings that remain. Do not change shared command blocking. Save before commit Evaluate drafts and reject blocking invalid values. Do not publish draft decisions. Save after commit Validate saved values in fresh runtimes, project decisions, and replay published state. A fresh runtime whose disposal fails again on its retry fails this validation after the replay; persisted values remain committed. Reset Commit defaults, apply them, validate, and publish. ISettingsPackSaveValidation.BlockSaveOnInvalid determines whether an invalid draft blocks Save. Invalid settings and a validation exception are different outcomes. Startup logs a validation exception without activating its feature warning. Settings-window failures propagate through the normal error path. Startup disposes every runtime it creates. It retries a failed disposal once, logs persistent failures with the pack identity, and preserves cancellation when cleanup also fails. The warning evaluator uses the same validated SettingsCatalog as the Settings window. Auto-update task integration ViewActivationTask<TSettings> reads the current settings once during admission. It returns no admission when AutoUpdateEnabled is false or any configured warning is active. Otherwise it evaluates the tool predicate and returns an admission that captures that settings snapshot. The hook distinguishes two failures: An admission failure records a document-session failure and activates WarningIdsToSetOnFailure. A settings-read failure occurs at this boundary. A failure while executing an admitted operation shows the canonical auto-update failure banner and suppresses further runs for that document session. It does not activate feature warnings automatically. Tool-owned prerequisite checks can activate a warning explicitly, for example when required shared parameters are missing. Unexpected runtime exceptions must propagate to the hook's safe-execution boundary. See Hooks for admission, document-session identity, and failure handling. An active warning can disable the editor's toggle through ToggleEnabled. Changing the persisted AutoUpdateEnabled preference is a separate tool policy. It is not a required side effect of SetWarning. Warning UI and command blocking SettingsWarningViewModel wraps an ISettingsPackRuntimeWarning. It exposes WarningId, Title, Message, IsActive, Clear and Fix commands, and Fix availability. The warning card binds to that row state. Publication reaches ribbon controls in this order: The warning service publishes a WarningChangedEventArgs. RibbonSettingsObserver receives the published change. RibbonVisualUpdater applies its per-command enabled state. RibbonCompositionState updates registered buttons. RibbonComposition registers controls before subscribing to settings changes. RibbonVisualUpdater also applies aggregate Settings-icon and tab-highlight updates. RibbonSettingsObserver owns subscription lifetime and dispatcher delivery. RibbonCompositionState owns the registered controls and panel state. Command preflight checks every applicable active warning. Ribbon enablement combines all active warnings for each command, so clearing one warning does not enable a button while another still blocks it. WarningChangedEventArgs carries WarningId, WarningTitle, PackKey, IsActive, and ToolInternalNamesToDisable. WarningSetChangedEventArgs carries aggregate HasWarnings. Treat these as published state, not persistence requests. Clearing and fixing warnings Clear sets the bound context warning false and calls ISettingsWarningService.SetWarning(id, false). It does not repair prerequisites or save settings. For view-activation tasks that declare the warning, clearing it releases their per-document failure gates so a later view activation can try again. A later validation or prerequisite check can activate the warning again. A tool can clear a warning programmatically after its prerequisite check succeeds: warnings.SetWarning("core.structural.combined_tags", false); Changing only a context property does not publish command availability. Use the service or the Settings validation workflow to synchronize published state. A context that implements IWarningFixProvider can add a Fix action: string FixWarningId { get; } string FixLabel { get; } Task FixWarningAsync(CancellationToken ct = default); The provider's warning ID must match the card. Blank IDs or labels fail construction. SettingsWarningViewModel invokes the provider, updates command state when the context changes, and logs action failures. Its ActionFailed event passes failures to Settings feedback. Disposal unsubscribes the context observer. Combined Foundation Tags uses Fix for Install/Repair. Its pack view loads the shared-parameter status when it is shown; its constructor only prepares editor state. Its background checks set the warning without a banner, and its commands offer Repair when they find invalid prerequisites. See Settings Packs for host context and persistence ordering. Examples Combined Foundation Tags uses core.structural.combined_tags for Update Combined Foundation Tags, Move Combined Tags, and Organize Foundation Types. Transfer Drafting Views uses core.library.invalid to report invalid saved paths in Settings. Import From Library and Export To Library open Select Library File while the warning is active. Joist Girder Weights uses core.structural.joist_girder for its update command. Their manifests under src/Tools/ define the IDs and messages. See Testing Tools for warning-service test procedures.

developer-guide/developing/hooks.html.title: Hooks | dbtools
developer-guide/developing/hooks.html.summary: Hooks Hooks attach tool behavior to Revit application events. Core's HookHost resolves registered implementations, owns the shared ViewActivated subscription, and coordinates initialization, rollback, and shutdown. Tool-owned lifecycle hooks manage subscriptions that need their own event adapters. Use IViewActivationTask for work triggered by a view change. Use IHookLifecycle for owned subscriptions such as contextual ribbon UI or dialog suppression. Register services through the tool module. Do not attach another copy of Core's ViewActivated handler. Hook architecture flowchart LR Revit[Revit events] --> Host[HookHost] Registry[ToolRegistry and DI] --> Host Host --> View[ViewActivationHook] Host --> Lifecycle[IHookLifecycle implementations] View --> Tasks[IViewActivationTask services] Core's AddDbtHookRuntimeServices registers the single ViewActivationHook service beside HookHost. The hook collects IEnumerable<IViewActivationTask> from DI; tools contribute tasks, not hook registrations. ViewActivationHookDispatcher owns the outer safe-execution boundary. ViewActivationTaskRunner evaluates admissions and executes admitted tasks. ToolRegistry records only lifecycle hooks, in registration order, through RegisterLifecycleHook<T>(). HookCatalog resolves the required ViewActivationHook service and each registered lifecycle implementation from the service provider. Resolution fails when the view-activation hook or a lifecycle service is missing, or when a lifecycle service does not implement IHookLifecycle. Hooks run in response to Revit UI callbacks. Returning Task does not move API work to a background thread. Use asynchronous I/O where appropriate, avoid blocking the UI, and reacquire a valid Revit call gate before API work after an await. Modularity describes the synchronous callback restriction. Registering hooks Register both the concrete service and its lifecycle registration: public override void RegisterServices(IServiceCollection services, ToolManifest manifest) { services.AddSingleton<ContextualEditHook>(); } public override void RegisterHooks(ToolRegistry registry, ToolManifest manifest) { registry.RegisterLifecycleHook<ContextualEditHook>(); } This excerpt assumes a tool-owned ContextualEditHook : IHookLifecycle whose constructor dependencies are registered. Manifest and module setup is described in Creating New Tools. View-activation tasks use a factory registration. The Elevation Tags task needs manifest warning IDs in addition to its registered service dependencies: var warning = manifest.GetSingleSettingsPack().GetSingleWarning(manifest.Id); var warningIds = new[] { warning.Id }; services.AddSingleton<ElevationTagAlignmentService>(); services.AddSingleton<IViewActivationTask>(sp => new AlignOnViewActivatedTask( sp.GetRequiredService<ISettingsProvider>(), sp.GetRequiredService<SettingsSection<ElevationTagsSettings>>(), sp.GetRequiredService<ISettingsWarningService>(), sp.GetRequiredService<ElevationTagAlignmentService>(), sp.GetRequiredService<IBannerNotifier>(), sp.GetRequiredService<ILogger<AlignOnViewActivatedTask>>(), warningIds)); This excerpt follows Elevation Tags' App/Composition/ServiceCollectionExtensions.cs. The IReadOnlyCollection<string> warningIds constructor argument comes from the manifest, not automatic DI resolution. Every task must have a nonblank unique TaskId. All entries in WarningIdsToSetOnFailure must match registered warning definitions. The task registry validates these identities at construction. The IViewActivationTask System The public contract separates admission from execution: public interface IViewActivationTask { string TaskId { get; } string DisplayName { get; } IReadOnlyCollection<string> WarningIdsToSetOnFailure { get; } Task<ViewActivationAdmission?> AdmitAsync( UIApplication uiapp, ViewActivatedEventArgs args, CancellationToken ct); } AdmitAsync returns null to skip the attempt. A non-null ViewActivationAdmission captures the state that attempt will use: new ViewActivationAdmission(executionCt => ExecuteAsync(snapshot, executionCt)); The hook invokes the returned admission callback once for that attempt. Create a new admission for each event so it captures that event's state. ViewActivationTask Derive from ViewActivationTask<TSettings> for an auto-update task with typed settings. TSettings must implement IAutoUpdateSettings and have a public parameterless constructor. Its base constructor receives: ViewActivationTask( ISettingsProvider settingsProvider, SettingsSection<TSettings> settingsSection, ISettingsWarningService warnings, IBannerNotifier notifier, ILogger logger, string taskId, string displayName, IReadOnlyCollection<string> warningIds); The base admission sequence is: Check cancellation and read the current typed settings. Skip when AutoUpdateEnabled is false. Skip when any configured warning is active. Call the optional ShouldRunInternalAsync predicate. Capture that settings snapshot in an admission calling ExecuteInternalAsync. Override these methods with the exact signatures: protected override Task<bool> ShouldRunInternalAsync( UIApplication uiapp, ViewActivatedEventArgs args, MyToolSettings settings, CancellationToken ct) { var view = args.CurrentActiveView; return Task.FromResult(view != null && (view.ViewType == ViewType.FloorPlan || view.ViewType == ViewType.CeilingPlan)); } protected override Task ExecuteInternalAsync( UIApplication uiapp, ViewActivatedEventArgs args, MyToolSettings settings, CancellationToken ct) { return _updater.UpdateAsync(uiapp, args.CurrentActiveView, settings, ct); } This excerpt assumes a tool-owned updater with that operation. Inject its real implementation. Filter cheap conditions before expensive work. Use shared transaction services for modifications and synchronous callbacks inside them. Do not create a transaction around asynchronous work. The base exposes Logger and a protected banner helper. It reads no settings again during execution, so the admitted values remain consistent and settings-read failures occur at admission. Dispatch and failure policy The hook resolves the document from args.CurrentActiveView and returns when there is no active document/view. It visits tasks in DI registration order. Each task is evaluated and executed through the safe executor. Outcome Result Null admission Skip the task for this event. Admission failure Record a document-session failure and activate the task's warning IDs. Execution failure Show the canonical auto-update failure banner and record a document-session failure. Do not automatically activate feature warnings. Cancellation Preserve the canceled outcome rather than classify it as a runtime failure. A runtime failure suppresses subsequent attempts for the task/document session. The gate uses DocumentSessionKey. Save As or the first save can create a new key, and reopening a document starts a new session. Clearing a feature warning alone does not erase the recorded runtime failure for that key. Tool prerequisite checks may explicitly activate an actionable warning and return without executing the update. Unexpected updater exceptions propagate. Feature Warnings owns the distinction between invalid configuration, admission failure, and execution failure. Core suppresses routine logs and presentation on the outer event dispatch. Admission uses error-only banners without start/completion logs. An admitted execution logs start/completion, suppresses generic executor banners, and uses one canonical runtime-failure banner. Keep detailed probes at Trace and log meaningful state changes. Do not suppress failure logs unless another published lifecycle owner observes and records that exact failure. IHookLifecycle Lifecycle hooks implement three operations: public interface IHookLifecycle { Task InitializeAsync(UIControlledApplication application, CancellationToken ct); Task RollbackAsync(UIControlledApplication application, CancellationToken ct); void Shutdown(UIControlledApplication application); } InitializeAsync acquires subscriptions and other owned state. If initialization fails partway, the implementation must undo its own partial work and preserve both initialization and cleanup failures. Record ownership immediately after subscription, before later logging or callbacks can fail. RollbackAsync reverses attachment when later startup work fails. It can queue into a valid Revit context because its continuation may run outside the original UI callback. Shutdown runs synchronously in Revit's shutdown callback. It must finish owned unsubscribe/removal work before returning. It has no cancellation token and cannot publish background work for later completion. Host ordering and rollback HookHost.AttachAsync resolves handlers, initializes lifecycle actions in registration order, then force-queues its ViewActivated subscription. It publishes attached state only after all actions succeed. The host records each attempted owner before initialization begins. Successfully initialized actions roll back in reverse order if attachment fails. The failing initializer owns its partial cleanup. Normal shutdown also reaches attempted owners whose initialization or rollback is incomplete. HookAttachAction cancels pending attachment, prevents later initialization or rollback dispatch after shutdown is requested, and makes completed shutdown idempotent. Cancellation failure does not prevent its shutdown callback. A failed callback remains available for retry. Late asynchronous attachment completion cannot invoke Revit shutdown callbacks from a background thread. HookLifecycleCoordinator attempts every reverse-order teardown action and aggregates contextual failures. Hooks and view tasks follow registration order. Group dependent operations in one hook or task when their ordering is part of the behavior. Contextual ribbon injectors dbtools.Core.Tools.Hooks.ContextualRibbon.ContextualRibbonInjector implements IHookLifecycle and IDisposable. Derive from it for tool-specific Edit buttons on contextual tabs. Super Girt Tool (SGT) supplies ContextualEditHook as an example. The derived type supplies tool/button/event names, the registered contextual command type, target tabs, selection evaluation, button construction, and edit flow. The base owns selection-change observation, injected controls, system-ID state, safe execution, and the edit ExternalEvent. Initialization queues API work to create the edit event, subscribe to selection changes, and evaluate the initial state. A partial failure immediately attempts unsubscribe, contextual UI removal, and edit-event disposal. Rollback uses the queued cleanup path. Normal shutdown uses synchronous cleanup and the exact detach action captured at successful subscription. Create ExternalEvent objects only in valid Revit API contexts. Autodesk ribbon command callbacks are not such a context. The base creates/refreshes its edit event through its managed Revit entry path. Contextual edit validates ContextualEditCommandType through CommandPreflight, sharing normal command registration and warning policy. Do not duplicate the base's event subscription or button registry in a derived type. FindTargetTabs, EvaluateSelection, BuildButton, and RunEditFlow are the tool-specific extension points. Synchronous shutdown Revit's IExternalApplication.OnShutdown is synchronous. AppLifecycleCoordinator.Shutdown invokes AppShutdownWorkflow.RunSynchronously through AppShutdownLifecycle.CleanupSynchronously in that callback. It cancels startup, detaches hooks, and disposes runtime hosts before returning. It disposes the startup cancellation source only when startup is complete or absent. It neither queues Revit work nor pumps the dispatcher. Unfinished startup or deferred observation yields Result.Failed after owned teardown attempts. Core owns WPF dispatcher operation tracking and retirement. See the dispatcher operation retirement contract. Logger, ribbon, notification, and progress work uses WpfDispatcher.Post or WpfDispatcher.Queue. See Core's dispatcher operation retirement contract for their callback and shutdown behavior. Extending and debugging hooks Use IHookLifecycle for another owned application subscription. Add an event-specific contract only when its dispatch shape requires one. Such a change must add its Core registration, resolution, subscription, safe-execution policy, rollback, synchronous detach, and tests together. ToolRegistry accepts only lifecycle hooks. Symptom Check Lifecycle hook never initializes Register both its concrete DI service and its RegisterLifecycleHook<T>() registration. View task never runs Check its IViewActivationTask registration, settings, active warnings, predicate, and document-session failure gate. Startup rejects the task Check nonblank unique task IDs and known warning IDs. Handler resolution fails Register the concrete type and its constructor dependencies. UI freezes Remove synchronous waits and long work from UI callbacks. Re-enter the gate for API work after an await. Cleanup fails Inspect contextual errors for each unsubscribe, UI removal, and disposal attempt. Inspect %APPDATA%/dbtools/Logs/ first. Use the Settings Debug Mode control for runtime diagnostics rather than adding an unrelated logging configuration. See Testing Tools for fixture placement, compilation, and execution commands.

developer-guide/developing/modularity.ht.title: Modularity | dbtools
developer-guide/developing/modularity.ht.summary: Modularity Tools use Core for execution, transactions, settings, logging, and window lifecycle. Presentation owns stable WPF shells, controls, resources, and themes. Tool assemblies own feature behavior, raw views, and ViewModels. Use constructor injection inside services. Resolve the first workflow from ICommandContext at the command boundary. Creating New Tools describes assembly ownership and module registration. Service lifetimes The application service root lasts for one runtime generation. A command or modeless session owns a run scope for Revit-dependent services. Service Lifetime Purpose ISafeExecutor Singleton Error policy, logging, and notifications at entrypoints. IAlertService Singleton Alert and selection dialogs. ISettingsProvider Singleton Fresh typed reads and atomic batch commits. ToolRegistry Application runtime Command and hook registrations. IRevitRunScope Scoped Current Revit application and document access. IRevitCallGate Scoped Synchronous API callbacks in a valid Revit context. ITransactionRunner Scoped Transactions for model changes. ITransactionGroupService Scoped Group health and commit/rollback. Use ILogger<T> through injection and context.Logger at command boundaries. The application logging host owns logger lifetime. Keep Document, UIDocument, and run-scope references within their command or session lifetime. Pass operation-specific document inputs or obtain verified current state from the run scope. Dispose the command/session scope only after its owned work and cleanup finish. Safe execution dbtools.Core.SafeExecution.Domain.ISafeExecutor defines two boundaries: Task RunAsync( Func<Task> action, ILogger logger, IBannerNotifier? notifier, SafeExecutionOptions opts, CancellationToken ct = default); Task<SafeExecutionResult> RunWithoutThrowingAsync( Func<Task> action, ILogger logger, IBannerNotifier? notifier, SafeExecutionOptions opts, CancellationToken ct = default); RunAsync reports, then rethrows, refusals, cancellations and failures. RunWithoutThrowingAsync records an explicit outcome for a caller that must contain failure, such as a Revit event callback. Both provide correlation IDs, timing, cancellation admission, exception logging, and configured notifications. ToolCommand already owns this boundary. Let workflow failures reach it. SafeExecutionOptions requires an operation name: var options = new SafeExecutionOptions("Inspect Model") { BannerMode = SafeExecutionOptions.Mode.ErrorOnly }; await executor.RunAsync(InspectAsync, logger, notifier, options, ct); Option Default Effect LogStart true Log entry. LogCompletion true Log completion. LogFailure true Log a failed operation. BannerMode SuccessAndError Show success/error banners, errors only, or neither. CorrelationId Unspecified Supply an existing execution correlation ID. ErrorBanner(name, logStart, logCompletion) selects error-only banners. SuppressFailurePresentation(name) suppresses banners and routine start/completion logs while retaining failure logging. Disable LogFailure only when an already-published lifecycle owner observes and logs that same fault. Preserve the failed Task. App composition supplies the default banner notifier to SafeExecutor for failure paths without a call-site notifier. Window error boundaries use IWindowErrorLogSurface and WindowErrorPresenter. Consumers depend on these contracts rather than constructing concrete logger or notification windows. Use structured log fields: logger.LogInformation("Processing {Count} elements in {Document}", count, document.Title); logger.LogError(exception, "Inspection failed for {Document}", document.Title); Use IAlertService for user decisions and IBannerNotifier for banners. Propagate failures through the safe-execution boundary with their context. Revit run scopes and call gates IRevitRunScope exposes UIApplication, CallGate, GetActiveUiDocument(), GetActiveDocument(), and GetVerifiedActiveDocument(expectedDocument, context). The verification method checks validity and DocumentSessionKey equality before returning the active document. Use the verification method before operating on a retained document. Run profile Gate Use InlineUi InlineRevitCallGate Commands already executing in a valid Revit API callback. QueuedModeless QueuedRevitCallGate Modeless work through the App-owned ExternalEvent host. The gate accepts synchronous callbacks: Task RunAsync(Action<UIApplication> work, CancellationToken ct = default, RevitCallGateMode mode = RevitCallGateMode.Auto); Task<T> RunAsync<T>(Func<UIApplication, T> work, CancellationToken ct = default, RevitCallGateMode mode = RevitCallGateMode.Auto); Await the returned Task outside the callback. Do not pass async lambdas into the gate. Async-state-machine Actions and known Task/ValueTask result shapes are rejected before execution. An awaitable hidden in object or an interface is rejected after the callback runs. Side effects remain. Custom awaiters are outside this check. A Revit API callback's context applies to its synchronous prefix. An async continuation must acquire a valid gate again before using the Revit API. InGate reports execution within a gate callback. It does not make arbitrary background work safe. On normal host retirement, pending queued work is dropped and its Tasks remain pending, even if cancellation arrives later. Shutdown must not await these Tasks. Failed-startup cleanup cancels pending work instead. See Revit execution for the full callback and shutdown contract. Transactions ITransactionRunner wraps synchronous model modifications: Task RunInActiveDocumentAsync(string name, Action<RevitTransactionContext> action, CancellationToken ct = default); Task<T> RunInActiveDocumentAsync<T>(string name, Func<RevitTransactionContext, T> action, CancellationToken ct = default); Task RunInDocumentAsync(Document doc, string name, Action<RevitTransactionContext> action, CancellationToken ct = default); Task<T> RunInDocumentAsync<T>(Document doc, string name, Func<RevitTransactionContext, T> action, CancellationToken ct = default); Use transaction.Document inside the callback: await transactions.RunInDocumentAsync(document, "dbtools - Set Mark", transaction => { var element = transaction.Document.GetElement(elementId); element.LookupParameter("Mark").Set(mark); }, ct); The runner selects a SubTransaction when the document is modifiable and a new Transaction otherwise. It enforces document context and applies TransactionFailurePreprocessor. The callback rules match the call gate: no async Actions or Task/ValueTask results. Give each transaction a descriptive undo name. Transaction groups ITransactionGroupService groups several transactions into one undo operation: bool IsActive { get; } Task BeginAsync(string name, CancellationToken ct = default); Task FinalizeAsync(TransactionGroupFinalization finalization, CancellationToken ct = default); Task<bool> IsGroupHealthyAsync(CancellationToken ct = default); Finalize with TransactionGroupFinalization.Commit to assimilate the group or Rollback to discard it. IsGroupHealthyAsync returns true when no group exists and false when an active group has lost its healthy started state. The session/workflow owner must finalize on success, failure, and cancellation. Use a separate cancellation token for cleanup when the operation is canceled. Attempt all owned cleanup and retain both the operation and finalization errors. Do not use an unguarded finally exception that hides the operation's failure. Long-lived tool sessions also own the ordering of persistence, window closure, group finalization, and scope disposal. Alerts and selection IAlertService.Show(AlertRequest) presents a request-based dialog. The AlertServiceExtensions methods in dbtools.Core.Alert.Workflow build the confirmation and selection requests and present them through Show: AlertResult Show(AlertRequest request); bool Confirm(this IAlertService alerts, string message, IWindowOwnerHandleProvider ownerHandleProvider, string title = "dbtools"); T? SelectSingle<T>(this IAlertService alerts, AlertSelectionRequest<T> request) where T : class; IReadOnlyList<T> SelectMultiple<T>(this IAlertService alerts, AlertSelectionRequest<T> request) where T : class; Confirmation requires an owner provider. In a command: var alerts = context.Resolve<IAlertService>(); if (!alerts.Confirm("Delete the selected elements?", context.OwnerHandleProvider)) return; Selection requests supply choices, a display function, window title, header, and owned window options. For example: var selected = alerts.SelectSingle(new AlertSelectionRequest<Level>( levels, level => level.Name, "Select Level", "Target Level", new AlertWindowOptions(context.OwnerHandleProvider)) { Message = "Choose the target level." }); Core owns selection policy, body construction, and typed result extraction; a test substitute implements Show only. Settings Inject ISettingsProvider and the typed SettingsSection<T>. Call Get(section) at the operation boundary for a fresh snapshot. Reads layer appsettings.json and the current per-year user file. Commit one or more section writes as a batch: var options = settings.Get(section); options.AutoUpdateEnabled = true; await settings.CommitAsync(new[] { section.CreateWrite(options) }, ct); Do not retain a settings snapshot in a singleton when subsequent operations need saved changes. Settings Packs owns DTO restrictions, source-generated metadata, file locking, save timing, and post-commit errors. Shared UI resources dbtools.Presentation.ThemeBrushKeys exposes ComponentResourceKey values. Use dynamic resources so the window's theme supplies each brush: <Border xmlns="http://schemas.microsoft.com/winfx/2006/xaml/presentation" xmlns:x="http://schemas.microsoft.com/winfx/2006/xaml" xmlns:theme="clr-namespace:dbtools.Presentation;assembly=dbtools.Presentation" Background="{DynamicResource {x:Static theme:ThemeBrushKeys.Surface}}"> <TextBlock Text="Inspection" Foreground="{DynamicResource {x:Static theme:ThemeBrushKeys.Body}}" /> </Border> Keys cover brand, surface, text, status, and DataGrid brushes. Use the actual members in ThemeBrushKeys.cs and tokens in Resources/Tokens.xaml. Do not invent string keys or duplicate color values. Window-scoped resources avoid changing another add-in's theme. See the Theme System. Merge the stable Presentation theme into a raw view through ResourceUri: <Grid xmlns="http://schemas.microsoft.com/winfx/2006/xaml/presentation" xmlns:resources="clr-namespace:dbtools.Presentation.Resources;assembly=dbtools.Presentation"> <Grid.Resources> <ResourceDictionary> <ResourceDictionary.MergedDictionaries> <ResourceDictionary Source="{resources:ResourceUri Resources/Theme.xaml}" /> </ResourceDictionary.MergedDictionaries> </ResourceDictionary> </Grid.Resources> </Grid> ResourceUri selects the loaded Presentation assembly's versioned resource URI. Keep raw views on stable resources rather than constructing payload pack URIs. Design tokens Resources/Tokens.xaml defines spacing, padding, corner radius, and typography. Use the token with the property type it expects: Token Type and value Spacing4, Spacing8, Spacing16 Thickness values of 4, 8, and 16. Spacing4.Value, Spacing8.Value, Spacing16.Value Double values for scalar properties. Pad8, Card.Padding Thickness values of 8 and 16,12. ButtonGap Thickness 8,0,0,0: space before each button after the first in a row. Size.Control Double value of 28 for the height of compact controls, including buttons in a DialogFooter. MinHeight.Button Double value of 28 for the minimum height of a themed button. Radius4, Radius8 CornerRadius values of 4 and 8. FontSize.Body, FontSize.Title, FontSize.Header Double values of 13, 15, and 20. Tool-window sessions A raw tool view uses framework or stable Presentation types. It has no Window root, x:Class, code-behind event attributes, tool CLR namespaces, payload BAML, or implicit templates for tool types. Bind display values explicitly. Core's ToolWindowFactory installs the theme, owner, icon, error boundary, and progress lifecycle before parsing. It registers the session for normal closure and runtime-generation retirement: using var xaml = new MemoryStream(ToolWindowXaml.ReadEmbeddedResource( typeof(MyToolWindowViewModel).Assembly, "dbtools.ToolViews.MyTool.MyToolWindow.xaml")); var session = factory.CreateModal(xaml, viewModel, new ToolWindowOptions { Title = "My Tool", Width = 800, Height = 600 }); _ = session.ShowDialog(); Use factory.CreateModeless(...) and session.Show() for a modeless surface. CreateModal returns IModalToolWindowSession with ShowDialog and HideForPick. CreateModeless returns IModelessToolWindowSession with Show. Both inherit the common lifecycle surface from IToolWindowSession. Register payload handlers and owned cleanup through the session. A custom initializeShell callback owns the initializer it creates and must register its disposal through session.AddCleanup. Normal close dispatches payload Closed handlers before releasing owned state. Retirement of an open session also clears its view graph. Keep the application run scope alive through failure-bearing session completion. Window.Close() alone does not establish that asynchronous cleanup finished. Presentation owns shells and ToolWindowCallbackScope. Core and tool assemblies can belong to a replaceable product generation. Stable controls and resources must not retain a retired ViewModel, callback, or tool type. This contract also applies to Settings, alerts, logger windows, banners, and progress UI. Sandbox Integration covers previews and native WPF validation. Hooks covers subscriptions that also need generation-safe shutdown.

developer-guide/developing/new-tool-guid.title: Creating New Tools | dbtools
developer-guide/developing/new-tool-guid.summary: Creating New Tools A dbtools tool owns its source, manifest, resources, production assembly, and tests. App discovers embedded manifests, registers services, and composes ribbon controls. Each tool assembly ships under the product year's Tools/ directory. Service and settings modules follow the same assembly contract as ribbon tools. Use this page to create the tool boundary. See Modularity for runtime services, Settings Packs for configuration, Hooks for events, and Testing Tools for validation. Prerequisites Run commands from the repository root. Desktop builds support Revit 2026 (2026.5 or later) and Revit 2027. Both use net10.0-windows. The selected year chooses API references and output directories. APS Design Automation uses a separate Revit 2026/.NET 8 contract. Check the build entrypoint before adding a tool: ./build.sh --help ./build.sh BuildApp -y 2026 On native Windows, use the PowerShell entrypoint: pwsh -NoProfile -File build.ps1 BuildApp -y 2026 build.sh supports Linux and WSL. It refuses native Windows shells. The wrappers acquire the SDK pinned in global.json when needed. Build and validation commands explains the targets, defaults, logs, and source gates. 1. Choose the owner and names Place a tool under src/Tools/<Category>/<Tool>/. Categories such as Common, Structural, Experimental, and Services organize source. They do not enter CLR namespaces. A tool's namespace root is dbtools.<Tool>. Follow the repository's .agents/canon/CANON.md naming contract: Mirror folders in namespaces beneath the component root. Give each C# identity its own file with the same name. Partial companions may use dotted suffixes, such as Workflow.Validation.cs. Put manifest-facing commands and modules under App/Composition/. Put whole-tool composition, windows, navigation, and session lifetime under App/. Put user capabilities under Features/<Concept>/ and shared tool language under Domain/. Put Revit adapters beneath the nearest owning concept's Revit/ folder. Create only populated owners. CANON bans Shell and Shared as production owners and treats Models as a generic kind bucket. For example: src/Tools/Common/MyTool/ ├── App/ │ ├── Composition/ │ │ ├── MyToolCommand.cs │ │ └── MyToolToolModule.cs │ ├── DesignTime/ │ │ └── MyToolWindowDesignTimeViewModel.cs │ ├── ViewModels/ │ │ └── MyToolWindowViewModel.cs │ └── Views/ │ └── MyToolWindow.xaml ├── Assets/ │ └── my_tool.png ├── Features/ │ └── Inspection/ │ └── InspectionWorkflow.cs ├── Settings/ ├── Tests/ ├── dbtools.MyTool.csproj └── manifest.yml The optional Settings/ and Tests/ entries represent actual content, not placeholder directories. Short tool prefixes use Pascal-compressed forms such as Gm, Sgt, and Tdv. Window names pair with their runtime and design-time ViewModels, for example GmWindow, GmWindowViewModel, and GmWindowDesignTimeViewModel. 2. Create the production project Every tool manifest root needs a production project with DBT_IsToolAssembly=true, including a module with no ribbon commands. Add production and test projects to dbtools.sln under the owning solution folder. This project is a starting point for the example tool's dbtools.MyTool.csproj: <Project Sdk="Microsoft.NET.Sdk"> <PropertyGroup> <TargetFramework>$(DBT_RevitTargetFramework)</TargetFramework> <DBT_RevitHostIdentity>$(DBT_DesktopRevitHostIdentity)</DBT_RevitHostIdentity> <DBT_IsToolAssembly>true</DBT_IsToolAssembly> <RootNamespace>dbtools.MyTool</RootNamespace> <ImplicitUsings>enable</ImplicitUsings> </PropertyGroup> <ItemGroup> <Compile Remove="Tests\**\*.cs" /> <ProjectReference Include="..\..\..\dbtools.Core\dbtools.Core.csproj" /> <PackageReference Include="Microsoft.Extensions.Logging.Abstractions" /> <EmbeddedResource Include="Assets\*.png"> <Link>Resources\Icons\%(Filename)%(Extension)</Link> </EmbeddedResource> </ItemGroup> </Project> The repository supplies year-specific Revit API metadata packages through Directory.Build.targets. Do not copy installed Revit DLLs into the product. Declare a direct, versionless package reference when source uses that package's API. Prefer the smallest package that supplies the API. When tests need internal production types, declare visibility in the tool project for the exact consuming assembly names: <ItemGroup> <InternalsVisibleTo Include="dbtools.MyTool.Pure.Tests" /> <InternalsVisibleTo Include="dbtools.MyTool.Local.Tests" /> </ItemGroup> Content-derived assembly identity applies by default to tool assemblies through build/MSBuild/ContentVersion.targets. This includes non-WPF tools. For WPF, add UseWPF=true, reference Presentation where used, and add CommunityToolkit.Mvvm when using its generators. Tool views are raw embedded XAML. Disable automatic Page compilation and give each raw resource an explicit logical name: <PropertyGroup> <UseWPF>true</UseWPF> <EnableDefaultPageItems>false</EnableDefaultPageItems> </PropertyGroup> <ItemGroup> <ProjectReference Include="..\..\..\dbtools.Presentation\dbtools.Presentation.csproj" /> <PackageReference Include="CommunityToolkit.Mvvm" /> <EmbeddedResource Include="App\Views\MyToolWindow.xaml" LogicalName="dbtools.ToolViews.MyTool.MyToolWindow.xaml" /> </ItemGroup> Tools with Revit-dependent designer source can exclude **\Revit\**\*.cs when DesignTimeBuild=true. Keep designer-only resource dictionaries separate from runtime raw views. If a project compiles Properties\DesignTimeResources.xaml, its Page metadata can declare SubType=Designer, Generator=MSBuild:Compile, and ContainsDesignTimeResources=true. 3. Declare the manifest A ribbon module can use this manifest: id: dbtools.MyTool assembly: dbtools.MyTool moduleType: dbtools.MyTool.App.Composition.MyToolToolModule order: 0 panel: Common tool: ribbonTools: - internalName: dbtools.MyTool commandType: dbtools.MyTool.App.Composition.MyToolCommand runProfile: InlineUi displayText: "My Tool" iconBaseKey: my_tool tooltip: "Inspect the active model" controlKind: PushButton order: 50 assembly is the actual simple assembly name. It does not end with .dll in any case and contains no /, \, , or :; the same rule applies to sandboxWindows assembly fields. App embeds manifests centrally, but compiles no tool source, XAML, or assets. The product build discovers declared tool projects and stages their assemblies under <year>/Tools/. build/MSBuild/ProductOutput.proj builds and stages those owners. ToolAssemblyResolver loads the declared file in the root assembly's owning context. Runtime resolves modules, commands, icons, and raw views from that owner. Manifest fields Field Requirement and meaning id Required unique tool identifier. assembly Required simple assembly name. moduleType Optional fully qualified ToolModule type. order Required load order, lower first. Use 0 without an ordering requirement. panel Required for every ribbon manifest and by settings-pack registration. Accepted values: Settings, Common, Structural, Testing, Services. tool.settings.configSection Optional single JSON property name in settings.<year>.json. tool.settingsPacks Optional pack definitions with required key and title. tool.ribbonTools Ribbon command definitions. May be absent for a service/settings/hook module. sandboxWindows Optional raw-view previews. See Sandbox Integration. A module must own at least one responsibility: ribbon tools, settings, settings packs, or registered lifecycle hooks. A moduleless manifest requires panel and at least one ribbon tool. It cannot declare settings or settings packs. For a service module, retain the project and declare its actual owner: id: dbtools.DialogSuppression assembly: dbtools.DialogSuppression moduleType: dbtools.DialogSuppression.App.Composition.DialogSuppressionToolModule order: -1 panel: Services tool: settings: configSection: Tools.DialogSuppression settingsPacks: - key: services.dialog_suppression title: "Dialog Suppression" Ribbon fields Field Requirement and meaning internalName Required unique control identity, also used by warning definitions. commandType Required fully qualified concrete ToolCommand type. availabilityType Optional separate type implementing IExternalCommandAvailability. Omit for command-owned availability. runProfile InlineUi by default, or QueuedModeless. displayText Required label. YAML double-quoted strings support \n line breaks. iconBaseKey Required embedded icon key without extension. tooltip Required tooltip text. controlKind PushButton by default, or SplitButtonItem, PulldownButtonItem, StackedButtonItem. group Required nonblank group for grouped controls. Invalid for a push button. order Required order within the panel/group. groupDisplayText Optional group header text. groupTooltip Optional group header tooltip. groupIconBaseKey Optional group header icon key. Optional values cannot be blank. Push buttons cannot carry grouped-control metadata. Entries in one panel with the same controlKind and group form one split button, pulldown button or stack, ordered by order. The lowest-order split entry is the primary command. The remaining entries are its dropdown commands. App planning and Revit construction use that sequence. Use a 32×32 main icon such as my_tool.png. An optional 16×16 companion is my_tool_16.png. Match the base filename to iconBaseKey. 4. Register services ToolModule lives in dbtools.Core.Tools.Modules.Composition. Its registration methods receive the manifest from dbtools.Core.Tools.Manifest: Method Contribution RegisterSettings Typed persistence sections. RegisterServices Tool services and dependency injection registrations. RegisterSettingsPacks Settings catalog definitions and context/view factories. RegisterHooks Lifecycle hook registrations in ToolRegistry. Startup calls RegisterSettings, RegisterServices, RegisterSettingsPacks, and RegisterHooks in that order for each module before validating and merging its registrations. Keep modules limited to composition. Put behavior with the feature that owns it. For example, a module can register a feature workflow: using dbtools.Core.Tools.Manifest; using dbtools.Core.Tools.Modules.Composition; using dbtools.MyTool.Features.Inspection; using Microsoft.Extensions.DependencyInjection; namespace dbtools.MyTool.App.Composition; public sealed class MyToolToolModule : ToolModule { public override void RegisterServices(IServiceCollection services, ToolManifest manifest) { ArgumentNullException.ThrowIfNull(services); ArgumentNullException.ThrowIfNull(manifest); services.AddScoped<InspectionWorkflow>(); } } A simple moduleless command may declare [CommandService(typeof(Workflow))] on the command. Framing Joins uses this pattern for FramingJoinsWorkflow. Do not reconstruct ribbon registrations in a module. App resolves concrete command and availability types. Core constructs their shared registrations. 5. Implement the command Use ToolCommand from dbtools.Core.Tools.Commands for ribbon commands. It supplies safe execution, contextual logging, command preflight, and scope creation/disposal. Revit constructs the command with an inert parameterless constructor. Resolve services inside RunAsync: using Autodesk.Revit.Attributes; using dbtools.Core.Tools.Commands; using dbtools.Core.Tools.Commands.Context; using dbtools.MyTool.Features.Inspection; namespace dbtools.MyTool.App.Composition; [Transaction(TransactionMode.Manual)] public sealed class MyToolCommand : ToolCommand { protected override Task RunAsync(ICommandContext context) { ArgumentNullException.ThrowIfNull(context); return context.Resolve<InspectionWorkflow>().ExecuteAsync(context.Document); } } This example assumes the feature defines InspectionWorkflow.ExecuteAsync(Document). The context exposes UIApplication, UIDocument, Document, Logger, OwnerHandleProvider, ShowErrorBanner, ShowWarningBanner, and inherited Resolve<T>(). Use the error banner for a failure and the warning banner for an expected refusal or a partial result. A documentless command overrides RequiresActiveDocument=false. Accessing its Document or UIDocument throws. Every ToolCommand implements IExternalCommandAvailability. Omit availabilityType to infer the concrete command. An explicit type equal to the command is rejected. A separate availability class uses an explicit type. The default predicate requires an open document unless RequiresActiveDocument is false. Override IsCommandAvailableCore for other predicates and use CommandAvailability methods such as HasActiveView, HasSelection, or HasCategorySelection. Pass HasCategorySelection the selectedCategories argument of IsCommandAvailableCore. Use the scoped ITransactionRunner for model changes. Its callbacks are synchronous, even though the entrypoint returns a Task. A modeless command uses the queued run profile and an owned session. See Modularity for call-gate, transaction, logging, and session contracts. 6. Add views, settings, and hooks A tool view embeds a stable element such as Grid. It has no x:Class, code-behind, tool CLR namespace, or event attributes. Presentation supplies the window shell. Core's ToolWindowFactory installs runtime services and registers its session. See Tool-window sessions. Use ObservableObject, [ObservableProperty], and [RelayCommand] from CommunityToolkit.Mvvm for bindable state and commands. Match the ViewModel's folder and namespace. Keep design-time ViewModels independent of Revit and production services. Sandbox Integration describes resource names, manifest declarations, visibility, and preview construction. For persisted options, define a DTO and a source-generated JSON context. Register one SettingsSection<T> and read it through ISettingsProvider. A settings pack adds the editor context and view. Settings Packs contains the complete registration and persistence sequence. For view-change work, register an IViewActivationTask service. For owned event subscriptions, implement IHookLifecycle and register the concrete service and its lifecycle registration. Hooks describes admission, failure handling, rollback, and synchronous shutdown. Feature Warnings describes configuration failures that disable commands. 7. Add tests and validate Tests live under the owning Tests/ directory and mirror production ownership: Tests/ ├── Features/Inspection/InspectionWorkflowTests.cs ├── Integration/Revit/Features/Inspection/InspectionWorkflowHostedTests.cs ├── Support/ ├── dbtools.MyTool.Pure.Tests.csproj └── dbtools.MyTool.Local.Tests.csproj Pure projects compile plain NUnit tests against the tool project. Local projects use explicit positive compile membership for [RevitLocal] fixtures and their support. A DA project claims coverage only through real APS WorkItem tests. Optional *.Portable.Pure.Tests projects exercise portable production targets on Linux. Keep the execution projects separate. Use focused commands during development: ./test.sh list --tool GM --scope pure --fixture DuplicateDetectionEngineTests ./test.sh test --tool GM --scope pure --fixture DuplicateDetectionEngineTests ./build.sh BuildSelectedLocalTests --TestProjects dbtools.GM.Local.Tests -y 2026 Replace GM with the new tool's directory key after its test projects exist. See Testing Tools for execution hosts and routing. Run the new tool's Pure fixtures through test.sh. Use Revit-hosted tests for ribbon composition and commands that need the Revit API. Use Windows Pure fixtures for WPF bindings, themes, and window cleanup. See Testing Tools for selection and execution commands.

developer-guide/developing/sandbox-integ.title: Sandbox Integration | dbtools
developer-guide/developing/sandbox-integ.summary: Sandbox Integration Sandbox previews tool windows and validates a staged distribution without starting Revit. Native validation runs on Windows and constructs real WPF windows. Run one fresh Sandbox process for each candidate year. Use this page to register a preview, build Sandbox, and run it on Windows. See Sandbox Validator for candidate loading, assembly boundaries, and the validation sequence. Portable build validation checks metadata, raw XAML, and Dev Mode policy on Linux. Native WPF validation and live Dev Mode injection require Windows. Register a window Declare a raw view in the tool's manifest.yml: sandboxWindows: - id: dbtools.MyTool.Main displayName: "My Tool" group: "Common" xamlResource: "dbtools.ToolViews.MyTool.MyToolWindow.xaml" windowKind: Modal width: 1200 height: 700 minWidth: 900 minHeight: 500 startupLocation: CenterScreen designTimeViewModelType: "dbtools.MyTool.App.DesignTime.MyToolWindowDesignTimeViewModel" designTimeViewModelAssembly: "dbtools.MyTool" designTimeViewModelVisibility: Public Embed the matching resource in the owning tool project: <EmbeddedResource Include="App\Views\MyToolWindow.xaml" LogicalName="dbtools.ToolViews.MyTool.MyToolWindow.xaml" /> Field Requirement and meaning id Required stable window identity. displayName Required catalog/window title. group Required catalog group. assembly Optional raw-view assembly override. Otherwise the tool's manifest owner. xamlResource Required exact embedded logical resource name. windowKind Modal by default, or Modeless. designTimeViewModelType Required fully qualified design-time type. designTimeViewModelAssembly Required simple assembly name. designTimeViewModelVisibility Required Public or Internal, matching the type. width, height, minWidth, minHeight Optional finite dimensions. Width/height must be positive. Minimum sizes may be zero. showInTaskbar Optional Boolean. Defaults to false. startupLocation Optional WPF startup location. Defaults to CenterOwner. titleBindingPath, titleStringFormat Optional title binding and format. The parser rejects unknown fields and blank required values. Use exact enum spellings. Multiple entries can share a design-time type while using different stable IDs and raw resources. The manifest owns this metadata. Sandbox does not infer a Window type from a filename. Raw views and runtime ownership Use a stable root such as Grid. Raw views have no Window root, x:Class, code-behind, event attributes, tool CLR namespaces, payload pack URIs, payload BAML, or implicit templates for tool types. Bind visible text, headers, items, and tooltips explicitly. Use explicit templates, selectors, and display paths for bound content. Use tool-window sessions to open the same raw view in the product. Settings pack views supplied by pack factories are a separate embedded editor surface. Design-time ViewModels A Public type needs a public parameterless constructor. An Internal type must be non-public and have a public or non-public parameterless constructor. The manifest must select the matching visibility. The type must be constructible. Keep construction independent of Revit documents, external events, network services, and production settings. namespace dbtools.MyTool.App.DesignTime; public sealed class MyToolWindowDesignTimeViewModel { public string Title => "My Tool"; public IReadOnlyList<string> Rows { get; } = new[] { "Example", "Preview" }; } Populate the ViewModel with sample state and commands. A display-only action can use NoOpCommand from dbtools.Core.UI.Commanding.DesignTime.NoOp. The Sandbox validator opens catalog windows with their design-time ViewModels and reports WPF binding errors. Use Global Mapper (GM) and Super Girt Tool (SGT) manifests under src/Tools/ as examples of raw-view and design-time ViewModel registration. Register additional validation cases Implement ISandboxWindowContributor on the tool module to validate additional window sessions or states in headless Sandbox. CreateWindowCases returns at least one SandboxWindowCase with a unique ID. Its Open callback creates a production session with sample inputs and an attached window error boundary. The optional Prepare callback runs after the session opens and checks any state specific to the case. Sandbox owns opening, closing and retiring the session. Register other owned resources with IToolWindowSession.AddCleanup. Implement ISandboxSettingsPackContributor when a settings pack's normal registration needs Revit data. RegisterSandboxSettingsPack registers the production pack with sample inputs in the Settings validation service provider. Sandbox uses the normal RegisterSettingsPacks for packs that can load off Revit. Build and run Build a product candidate and Sandbox: ./build.sh AssembleDistributionCandidate -y 2026 ./build.sh BuildSandbox -y 2026 Candidate assembly can compile edited source. Acceptance targets require a clean committed tree. Read the build output for its build ID and use that invocation's candidate directory: .artifacts/.staging/<build-id>/distribution-candidate/Release/2026/ .artifacts/sandbox/Release/2026/net10.0-windows/ Run Sandbox on Windows with the matching Revit year installed. Both modes resolve that installation, require its runtime files, and check metadata/runtime compatibility. Run these commands from the repository root: dotnet run --project src/dbtools.Sandbox/dbtools.Sandbox.csproj -p:RevitYear=2026 -- --dist-dir .artifacts/.staging/<build-id>/distribution-candidate/Release/2026 Replace <build-id> with the ID printed by the candidate build. To validate without the interactive catalog, add headless mode and the matching installed Revit reference directory: dotnet run --project src/dbtools.Sandbox/dbtools.Sandbox.csproj -p:RevitYear=2026 -- --headless --dist-dir .artifacts/.staging/<build-id>/distribution-candidate/Release/2026 --revit-reference-dir 'C:\Program Files\Autodesk\Revit 2026' These are native Windows commands. Daemon-routed acceptance uses its hidden desktop. See Testing Tools for routing. Options Sandbox [--dist-dir PATH] [--headless --revit-reference-dir PATH] Option Default and behavior --dist-dir PATH .artifacts/dist/Release. Accept a year directory or a root containing supported year directories. --headless Disabled. Run native validation without the interactive catalog. --revit-reference-dir PATH Required with --headless. Invalid without it. Both path options also accept --name=value. Blank values and unknown arguments fail. A distribution root selects the newest supported year containing dbtools.dll. It does not reject a root merely because both years are present. Use an explicit year directory to select 2026 when 2027 also exists. A missing candidate fails before WPF startup. Headless mode suppresses interactive UI but still creates native WPF windows, checks layout and bindings, exercises supported interactions, and closes owned windows. It requires Windows Desktop. It is not a Linux metadata-only mode. Package native validation inputs Run PackageSandboxValidationInput to package the current candidate and Sandbox for Windows distribution acceptance: ./build.sh PackageSandboxValidationInput This target requires a clean committed source tree and every supported year. Sandbox output and archive paths include the year: .artifacts/sandbox/<configuration>/<year>/<tfm>/ sandbox/<year>/<sanitized-tfm>/ Use the archive with the distribution acceptance command. For validation checks, failure handling, and the distinction between portable, native, and live Dev Mode validation, see Sandbox Validator. Troubleshooting Failure Action Missing view resource Match xamlResource to the owning project's LogicalName. ViewModel construction failure Check assembly/type names, declared visibility, and parameterless constructor access. Binding errors Read binding-listener output and supply explicit display bindings. Candidate file/identity mismatch Rebuild the selected candidate and inspect its recursive file set. Wrong candidate year Pass an explicit year directory rather than the distribution root. Reference mismatch Supply matching installed-year Revit references in headless mode. Cleanup failure Inspect the window/session cleanup failure before terminating the process. See Sandbox Validator, Assembly Loading, and Creating New Tools.

developer-guide/developing/settings-pack.title: Settings Packs | dbtools
developer-guide/developing/settings-pack.summary: Settings Packs A settings pack supplies a tool's editor in the dbtools Settings window. It binds a typed settings section, an editor context, a WPF view, and optional warnings. Packs appear as cards grouped by their registered ribbon panel. ISettingsProvider reads current settings and commits section batches. SettingsWindowViewModel owns Save and Reset through SettingsPersistenceWorkflow. Pack contexts edit state and validate it. They do not save independently. Files and typed sections The default user file is %APPDATA%/dbtools/settings.<year>.json. AppPaths.GetSettingsFile(revitYear) returns it for the year that App bootstrap receives and rejects a year outside 2015-2100 with ArgumentOutOfRangeException. The dbtools.AppPaths.BaseDir AppContext value relocates the base directory for the process; App startup sets it from DBT_USER_DATA_DIR. SettingsSectionReader reads appsettings.json from its base directory, then overlays the user file. An absolute user path is used directly. A relative one resolves against the base directory. The reader validates files at construction and reads both layers again on every Get. It retains no file watchers or open handles. A section is one JSON property, such as Tools.FoundationTags. Its name must be nonblank and cannot contain :. It is not a nested configuration path. Section and property lookup is case-insensitive. { "Tools.MyTool": { "AutoUpdateEnabled": true, "FamilyPattern": "^Example$" } } Register generated System.Text.Json metadata with the section as JsonTypeInfo<T>. The same metadata reads options and serializes writes: using System.Text.Json.Serialization; using dbtools.Core.Settings.Domain; namespace dbtools.MyTool.Settings; public sealed class MyToolSettings : IAutoUpdateSettings { public bool AutoUpdateEnabled { get; set; } = true; public string FamilyPattern { get; set; } = "^Example$"; } Place its JSON context in a separate matching file: using System.Text.Json.Serialization; namespace dbtools.MyTool.Settings; [JsonSerializable(typeof(MyToolSettings))] internal partial class MyToolSettingsJsonContext : JsonSerializerContext { } IAutoUpdateSettings requires only AutoUpdateEnabled. HasWarning belongs to editor/session state and must not be added as a persisted warning flag. Keep DTO graphs independent of Revit and UI state. The allowed leaf types are bool, string, and double.
