SharedParameterMigration.Migrate(document, source, target, requiredCategories, useHandling) replaces the project parameter source with the shared parameter target that has another GUID, for example a parameter that a project received from an older shared parameter file. target is an ExternalDefinition from the open shared parameter file; the file stays open until Migrate returns, and the project must not bind the target GUID. Loaded families may define it already; Migrate then binds that parameter. The caller supplies its own definitions and categories and selects useHandling explicitly. RemoveWithParameter deletes dependent schedule fields and filter rules with the source. CarryToTarget snapshots and restores supported schedule and filter uses. Migrate changes the project only when it can carry over every value. Before any change it: Refuses a global parameter, and refuses unless the source spec NameEquals the target spec. The message names both specs, for example 'Associated Pier Elevation' exists as Area; expected Length; nothing changed. Refuses when a rebar container overrides the source; the override cannot be carried to the target. Plans one write per value, read by storage type (String, Double, Integer, ElementId); unset values are skipped. An instance-bound source keeps each element value. A type-bound source copies each type value to every instance of that type in the bound categories; it refuses when a type has a value and no instance. When the target already exists, it also records target-only values on elements in categories added to the target binding. When loaded families define the target already, the binding makes source and target one parameter. Each element keeps the value that is not empty: an old value is written to the target, a target-only value is restored if binding changes it, and an element that has one value for the source and another for the target refuses. Compares the source definition with the target: name, visibility, hide-when-no-value, and, through an element that has the parameter, description and user-modifiable. The target is canonical; each difference is reported and logged. When a refusal lists an element, the message shows Family : Type or the element name, followed by the element ID. One transaction group then contains these operations: Delete the source. Bind the target as an instance parameter of the source categories and requiredCategories, in the source parameter group. Set its variance between group instances to the source's and verify it. Restore the recorded schedule fields and view filter trees when useHandling is CarryToTarget. Write every planned value to its element, then read each one back. Revit refuses a changed value on a member of a group placed more than once (directly or through a nested group) when the parameter does not vary between group instances ("Changes to groups are allowed only in group edit mode"), and the API has no group edit mode. When the source does not vary and a planned write changes such a value, step 1 also turns the variance on. A third transaction turns it off after the writes; Revit reports every element whose value it aligned with another instance of its group, and any such element, or any value read back afterwards that differs, rolls the group back. A source that does not vary holds one value per group member, so its values come back unchanged. Revit does not let every spec vary: in Revit 2026 and 2027 Text, Area, Material and URL can vary, and Integer, Number, Length and Yes/No cannot. For a spec that cannot vary, such a value is refused in the plan, before any change, and the message lists the grouped elements. A target-only value that a loaded family exposes on a member of a group placed more than once is the same in every placement, because Revit refuses another value while the parameter does not vary. The binding keeps it, so it needs no write and does not refuse, for any spec. Revit reports whether a parameter can vary only when variance is set. For Migrate and copied type values in Rebind, the plan trial-binds when the original binding does not vary and a candidate write is on a repeated group member. It checks whether the parameter can vary only if binding changes the value and a write is needed. The trial runs in a transaction (or a subtransaction inside an open transaction) that always rolls back. CheckMigrate and CheckRebind therefore find this refusal too. The trial binds the parameter in the same transaction, so its rollback leaves no dead binding key (see below). The API cannot create attached detail groups or design options, so those are not tested. If any write or read-back fails (read-only, rejected by Revit, a Revit exception, a grouped value that Revit aligned), or any step throws, the group rolls back and the project keeps the source with its binding and values. A write that Revit blocks for any other reason takes the same path. A refusal, or a rollback after failed writes, throws SharedParameterMigrationException; its Failures list each value that could not be carried over as a SharedParameterValueFailure with the element ID and reason, and each is logged as a warning. Any other failure propagates its own exception after the rollback. A caller with more repair steps runs Migrate inside its own transaction group, which then rolls the migration back with the rest. CarryToTarget records every field in each affected main and embedded schedule. It also records field order, formatting, display settings, sort and group entries, filters and percentage references. It blocks a combined field and a schedule with a calculated field; Revit counts a percentage field as a calculated field. After it replaces the parameter, it restores the target field at the source index and remaps the field IDs in every reference. It writes a display type (totals or minimum and maximum values) only when the restored field shows another one, because Revit rejects any such write on a field that cannot show it, and it refuses when the restored field cannot show the recorded display type. It reads the schedule back and compares the complete record. It also records each affected filter's categories, logical tree, inversion flags and typed rules. It rebuilds each tree with the target parameter ID, checks that every rule applies to the filter categories and compares the result with the record. An unknown rule or evaluator blocks the move. Any difference beyond the source-to-target parameter and field-ID substitutions throws inside the group and rolls the move back. CheckMigrate runs the same carry checks without a lasting change. An unplaced family type parameter stays on its type because the instance binding does not change it. CheckMigrate(document, source, target, requiredCategories, useHandling) and CheckRebind(document, parameter, requiredCategories) run the same checks and plan without a change, and throw the same refusals, so a caller can find every refusal before it changes the project. Revit registers each shared parameter of a loaded family in the project as a SharedParameterElement. When the project deletes that element (as Migrate and a delete of a duplicate do), Revit also removes the parameter from the labels of the loaded families that use it, so a tag shows no value. A caller therefore replaces the parameter in the families first, and deletes the old GUID only when nothing in a family uses it. SharedParameterFamilyMigration does that for any set of definitions. A family matches a target by name, ignoring case. FindFamilyNames(document, name, targetGuid) opens no family. It returns the loaded families whose types, or placed elements for an instance parameter, show a shared parameter with the name and another GUID where no project binding of that parameter to the family's category explains it. A direct-use path refuses when a non-editable nested family could hide another use. SharedParameterFamilyTarget.MoveDirectLabels is false by default. SketchDimensionRefusal accepts only such a dimension: an OST_WeakDims dimension without a family parameter label that references at least one former member, and otherwise only former members and elements that the family keeps. Revit manages these dimensions and can drop or add them on any regeneration, so Core neither deletes them nor counts them after the reload. A group also lists the sketch and sketch plane of a member among its members (IsPart), and Revit can replace them, so the recorded members leave them out. Each must belong to another member of its group (PartOwner: the sketch's owner or one of its elements, a curve in the sketch plane, the owner of a sketch in that plane, or an element that Revit deletes with it). An assigned zero or No counts as a value; only the type, name and category fields that Revit derives (s_structuralGroupParameters) do not. Its message names the family and the groups (SharedParameterLabels.DescribeGroups, for example 'Inner' (nested in 'Outer')) and says what to change in the family. Before the commit it checks that every former group member still exists outside any group with the same class, category, owner view ID and location: a text or label by its insertion point and direction, a location point with its rotation where Revit gives one, a curve by its end points and midpoint, or else the bounding box in the owner view. A failed direct-label trial is a Label hand-fix refusal. Rest is the remaining elapsed time. A run without Revit calls logs only elapsed time. checks the token immediately before it invokes the action inside the protected boundary, so pre-canceled work returns a canceled result without running; logs full exception details, including inner exceptions and XAML parse context. When a failed run has no notifier, it uses the App's default. It logs notifier failures. FailureDetails.Format supplies the exception message followed by the base exception message when that differs. A blank result shows The operation failed.. The Error banner offers Details; shows each failure once (Failure/FailureReport). When it shows a failure or refusal banner, it records that with the exception. The banner system keeps every request it accepts (see Notification banners). An outer layer that receives a recorded exception (or a wrapper or aggregate whose causes are all recorded) logs it and shows no banner. Records belong to the report scope that the outermost run of an asynchronous flow opens (an AsyncLocal). The outermost RunAsync, which rethrows, hands its record on to the window error boundary, which takes it once. A later run ignores and removes a record that another run handed on, so a failure that its caller cached and throws again in a later run is shown again. A cached failure that reaches the boundary without a run is still taken as shown once. Code that shows its own failure banner and rethrows calls FailureReport.ShowBanner; a last handler calls FailureReport.TakeShown; reports, then rethrows, refusals, cancellations and failures from RunAsync(...). The rethrown exception keeps its instance and stack trace, unless a reporting failure wraps it in an AggregateException with the operation's exception first. RunWithoutThrowingAsync(...) returns the same outcome as a SafeExecutionResult, for event and UI callers that log and notify, then stop propagation. A null argument faults the task of either method. The XML documentation of ISafeExecutor gives the full contract. An expected refusal throws SafeExecutionRefusedException; the result status is SafeExecutionStatus.Refused and SafeExecutionRefusalReporter reports it once: the first layer with a notifier shows the warning banner, and outer layers only log it. An explicit separate availability type uses the existing resolver and validation route. An explicit type equal to the command type is rejected with tool and command context. The direct registration constructor retains nullable availability metadata. CommandAvailabilityValidator.Validate(...) reuses the executing instance when its exact type and the registered availability type equal the command type. Contextual edits have no executing command instance, so the validator constructs the declared availability type once. It also constructs separate availability classes once. Null availability metadata skips the check. Both paths create the Revit category set and use the same refusal messages. ToolModule public abstract class ToolModule { public virtual void RegisterSettings(IServiceCollection services, ToolManifest manifest) { } public virtual void RegisterServices(IServiceCollection services, ToolManifest manifest) { } public virtual void RegisterSettingsPacks(IServiceCollection services, ToolManifest manifest) { } public virtual void RegisterHooks(ToolRegistry registry, ToolManifest manifest) { } } public class MyToolModule : ToolModule { public override void RegisterServices(IServiceCollection services, ToolManifest manifest) { services.AddSingleton<IMyService, MyService>(); services.AddSingleton<IViewActivationTask, MyViewActivatedTask>(); } public override void RegisterHooks(ToolRegistry registry, ToolManifest manifest) { registry.RegisterLifecycleHook<MyContextualRibbonInjector>(); } } ToolRegistry The registry of tool registrations and lifecycle hooks. Command execution reads registration metadata through CommandPreflight; HookCatalog resolves the lifecycle hooks in registration order. public sealed class ToolRegistry { public ReadOnlyCollection<ToolRegistration> Tools { get; } public IReadOnlyList<Type> LifecycleHookTypes { get; } public bool HasHookRegistrations { get; } public void RegisterTool(ToolRegistration registration); public ToolRegistration ResolveCommandRegistration(Type commandType); public void RegisterLifecycleHook<T>() where T : class, IHookLifecycle; public void MergeFrom(ToolRegistry source); } RegisterLifecycleHook<T>() rejects a type that is already registered. MergeFrom checks every incoming tool and lifecycle hook against the target before it changes the target, then appends the source registrations after the target's. The registry has no view-activation entry: Core's AddDbtHookRuntimeServices registers the one ViewActivationHook service. App owns assembly loading and the validation of command and availability types. With the concrete types resolved, ToolRegistration.FromManifest(...) builds the registration and the registry accepts it. ToolRegistration and ToolRibbonSpec public sealed class ToolRegistration { public Type CommandType { get; } public Type? AvailabilityType { get; } public AppRunScopeProfile ExecutionProfile { get; } // manifest RunProfile; default InlineUi public ToolRibbonSpec Ribbon { get; } public static ToolRegistration FromManifest(Type commandType, ToolManifest manifest, RibbonToolManifest tool, Type? availabilityType = null); } ToolRibbonSpec is the Revit-free ribbon metadata that App ribbon composition consumes. FromManifest(...) is the only place that holds both the tool manifest and the ribbon manifest. It selects the internal ToolRibbonSpec.CreatePushButton(...) or CreateGroupedControl(...) factory and keeps the manifest display text and group metadata. A push control cannot carry group fields; a grouped control requires a non-push control kind and a non-blank group identity. Hooks Supported hook types: ViewActivationHook: the Core dispatcher for view-activated work. AddDbtHookRuntimeServices registers it; IViewActivationTask services supply its work. IHookLifecycle: module-owned lifecycle work, such as contextual ribbon setup or dialog-showing event subscriptions, registered through ToolRegistry.RegisterLifecycleHook<T>(). internal sealed class HookHost { internal Task AttachAsync(UIControlledApplication application, CancellationToken ct); internal Task RollbackAttachAsync(CancellationToken ct); internal void Detach(); } IHookLifecycle defines asynchronous initialization, asynchronous rollback after an attach failure and synchronous shutdown at the application boundary. Shutdown has no cancellation token or task; HookShutdownAction holds a plain Action. HookCatalog resolves the required ViewActivationHook service and the registered lifecycle implementations, in registration order, from DI. A missing service fails attachment. HookHost adds its own ViewActivated subscription as the last HookAttachAction, queues subscription and the unsubscription after an attach failure through the call gate, and publishes the attached state only after the whole attach succeeds. HookLifecycleCoordinator keeps the attach actions that initialized successfully, rolls them back in reverse order after a later attach failure and runs their shutdown actions in reverse initialization order. Normal detach clears that ownership only after every action succeeds; after a failure the complete, idempotent action set stays available for retry. Each lifecycle implementation cleans up its own resources when its initialization fails after it acquired them. ViewActivationHookDispatcher owns the safe-executor dispatch policy for this high-frequency event. ViewActivationHook keeps a runtime-failure gate per task and per document. The gate keys on DocumentSessionKey (title, path and instance hash): a reopened model starts clean, and after Save As or the first save of a new model the task can run once more under the new key. Dialog Suppression records ownership immediately after its adapter subscribes and calls its unsubscribe path if later initialization fails. Contextual ribbon: Initialization cleanup runs in the queued initialization context. It attempts the selection detach, every contextual UI removal and the edit-event disposal, and keeps both the initialization and the cleanup failures. Each registration keeps its tab, panel and button, and whether the injection created the panel or only the button. Cleanup removes a panel only when it owns it; a reused panel loses only the created button. A foreign button with the same ID, and its handler, are kept. The injection registry removes only registrations that cleaned up successfully, keeps failed ones for retry and throws one aggregate after it attempts them all. Injection and button-state sweeps attempt every target, keep the original causes with their tab, panel and button, and throw one aggregate after the sweep. The selection controller keeps the exact detach action captured at subscription, so shutdown needs no new UIApplication. The selection refresh completion callback runs only after all injection, toggle or cleanup changes succeed. OnEvaluateAndToggleCompleted is an extension point of ContextualRibbonInjector; the Extreme Roof Framing Tool (ERFT) overrides it. Sources: src/dbtools.Core/Tools/Hooks/{Lifecycle,Host,ContextualRibbon}/, src/Tools/Services/DialogSuppression/Features/DialogSuppressionHook.cs. UI components Color picker ColorPickerViewModel synchronizes RGB, HSV and hex before raising ColorChanged. A component edit inside the callback synchronizes state and notifies PreviewBrush and HueBrush again. A notification guard suppresses nested ColorChanged events. Callback exceptions propagate. Invalid hex text remains visible without changing the color state or raising the event. Windows Presentation (dbtools.Presentation.Windows) owns the stable window surface: WPF Window inheritance, owner-handle support through IWindowOwnerHandleTarget and the IThemeOptOut contract. public class ModalWindow : Window, IWindowOwnerHandleTarget, IThemeOptOut { public IWindowOwnerHandleProvider? OwnerHandleProvider { get; set; } public bool UseDefaultTheme { get; set; } } public class ModelessWindow : Window, IWindowOwnerHandleTarget, IThemeOptOut { /* same members */ } ToolWindowHost constructs the stable shell. Core's ToolWindowFactory installs the owner, theme, icon, error boundary and progress lifecycle before the raw view loads; for a modeless window the session's shell initializer selects the modeless owner policy. Retiring the session releases all of it. Settings, Alert, Logger and notification banners are raw views hosted by ToolWindowSession. ToolWindowFactory registers modal Settings and Alert sessions and modeless Logger sessions in the window registry. The banner host registry retires its modeless sessions when banners close or reset. Sandbox previews load the same raw resources with manifest-declared design-time view models. ToolWindowRegistry.RetireAll retires child sessions first, then each session's registered cleanups, then closes the shell. App shutdown calls it before other runtime owners reset. Window error boundary dbtools.Core.UI.Windows.ErrorBoundary holds the window error workflow. WindowStaticRuntime.Configure(...) is the one composition point where App startup supplies the banner notifier. The runtime receives IWindowErrorLogSurface for a banner's Details action and IWindowErrorBanner for handled-error feedback, without depending on the concrete shells. WindowErrorBoundaryRegistry owns one exception subscription per dispatcher. It routes each failure to the most recently activated attached window, then through activation history, then the attached list, skipping windows that have closed. WindowErrorBoundary classifies the original exception and every nested branch, including every aggregate branch. A branch is a dbtools failure when its throwing method or a frame on its stack belongs to an assembly named exactly dbtools or starting with dbtools. (ordinal). Vendor code qualifies only as dbtools.Presentation, which merges Helix. A raw HelixToolkit* or other UI library assembly belongs to another add-in and never qualifies. A framework or Revit API failure raised from dbtools code is therefore handled; another add-in's vendor failure is not. A bare dbtools OperationCanceledException whose token was canceled is marked handled with a Warning log only: no banner and no handled-failure signal. The boundary presents and publishes the original outer exception, with its wrappers and causes, and returns the handled decision to the registry. An exception tree with no dbtools branch stays unhandled and gets no notification. A window seen as closed keeps a weak tombstone and cannot be attached again. A closed WPF window that was never attached or seen is outside this registry; classifying it would need reflection or a new HWND. A lifecycle owner can subscribe through WindowErrorBoundaryRegistry to the handled-failure signal of its window. The subscription requires the attached per-window host and throws if it is missing. The notification carries the original failure and any presentation failure. Detaching clears the window's observers. WindowErrorPresenter owns the banner policy. A failure whose record a run or tool handed on (see FailureReport) is only logged, and the record is taken. A SafeExecutionRefusedException shows its reason in a warning banner, without the logger window and never as Unhandled UI exception. Any other failure shows an Error banner with a Details button. Clicking it opens the logger window and enables Debug Mode. WindowStaticRuntime configures and resets Core UI for App and Sandbox. It serializes the whole lifecycle and reports ready only after diagnostics, window error boundaries and progress overlays are all configured. It rejects duplicate or partial existing configuration before it changes anything. A failed configuration rolls back only what that attempt installed, in reverse order, so it can be retried; cleanup failures are kept with the primary failure. Configure opens the dispatcher operation registry last, just before it reports ready. Reset retires that registry first, then resets error boundaries, progress overlays and diagnostics. It attempts every step, clears readiness even when a step fails and reports cleanup failures in one aggregate. The progress-overlay capability owns its host registry and visual attachment, so this reset disposes every registered host. App shutdown calls Reset after runtime host teardown. The Sandbox calls it when its window-runtime registration is disposed. The progress capability exposes only a getter for the attached overlay-visibility state, so tool XAML can collapse airspace content. WindowRuntimeCapabilities.CreateSandbox(writeLog, defaultOwnerMode) builds the Sandbox logger factory, logger, error-log surface, notification surface and a no-op progress capability inside the Core that owns the window interfaces. App startup configures its own notification, logging and progress capabilities with WindowOwnerMode.DefaultOwner. Sandbox installs WindowOwnerMode.Unowned. This required policy controls default-owner binding; explicit per-window owner providers retain their existing behavior. Sources: src/dbtools.Core/UI/Windows/Runtime/{WindowRuntimeCapabilities,WindowStaticRuntime}.cs, src/dbtools.Core/UI/Dispatching/DispatcherOperationRegistry.cs, src/dbtools.App/Shutdown/AppShutdownWorkflow.cs, src/dbtools.Sandbox/Runtime/WindowStaticRuntimeConfigurator.cs, src/dbtools.Sandbox/Composition/AppRuntime.cs. Alerts public interface IAlertService { AlertResult Show(AlertRequest request); } public static class AlertServiceExtensions { public static bool Confirm(this IAlertService alerts, string message, IWindowOwnerHandleProvider ownerHandleProvider, string title = "dbtools"); public static T? SelectSingle<T>(this IAlertService alerts, AlertSelectionRequest<T> request) where T : class; public static IReadOnlyList<T> SelectMultiple<T>(this IAlertService alerts, AlertSelectionRequest<T> request) where T : class; } AlertServiceFactory, IAlertService and AlertServiceExtensions are public. Show is the only presentation call, so a substitute implements Show alone. AlertServiceExtensions owns the confirmation request (buttons yes and no) and, through the internal AlertSelectionPolicy, the selection requests (buttons ok and cancel) and their typed results. An empty selection returns null or an empty list without calling Show. The internal AlertService, AlertBodyBuilder, AlertWindowPresenter and AlertWindowViewModel own presentation, body composition, modal display and shell state. Confirm takes an IWindowOwnerHandleProvider; other alerts take owner and size policy in AlertWindowOptions. Implement IAlertBody for custom alert content. Core's container bodies (composite, banner table and message selection) return their immediate children through the internal IAlertBodyChildren; AlertWindowPresenter walks them root first, and each IAlertBodyTemplateProvider that owns a body adds its templates once. AlertCompositeBodySpec rejects an undefined CompositeBodyLayout. Alerts and other explicitly sized CenterOwner tool windows use the owner's current Win32 window rectangle and monitor work area. This centers an alert over a maximized native owner even when its restore rectangle is on another monitor. ToolWindowHost uses the owner monitor's DPI to clamp the initial and minimum sizes. It moves the HWND to the target monitor before the window opens. WPF applies the window size in device-independent units and handles DPI changes. At Loaded, the host centers the final rectangle in Win32 screen coordinates. The window can resize on another monitor. If no WPF owner window is available, the native owner HWND remains set. Structural preview dbtools.Presentation.StructuralPreview.IStructuralPreview3D owns structural preview navigation and rendering. ERFT and the Super Girt Tool (SGT) pass immutable scene and emphasis snapshots and consume stable pointer events. Core compiles against Presentation; the Helix and SharpDX assets are private to Presentation. Each tool registers the viewport's synchronous disposal as a session cleanup. ToolWindowRegistry.RetireAll releases the viewport handlers, timers, camera, material and device state and payload subscriptions before it closes the shell. See Structural Preview. Extension points Call gates: implement IRevitCallGate for another execution mode. Hooks: register IHookLifecycle implementations, or IViewActivationTask services for view-activated work. Settings packs: register packs through AddDbtSettingsPackDefinition<TOptions, TContext>. Alert bodies: implement IAlertBody. Related pages Architecture Overview dbtools.App

developer-guide/projects/presentation.ht.title: dbtools.Presentation | dbtools
developer-guide/projects/presentation.ht.summary: dbtools.Presentation dbtools.Presentation.dll is the WPF assembly that stays loaded for the life of the Revit process. It is staged at the root of each product year, beside dbtools.dll and dbtools.Core.dll. Item Value Project src/dbtools.Presentation/dbtools.Presentation.csproj Assembly dbtools.Presentation.dll Target framework net10.0-windows (Revit 2026 (2026.5 or later) and Revit 2027) References WPF. Presentation owns the merged Helix, Serilog and Microsoft.Extensions logging, dependency injection, options and primitives libraries. Contents Presentation holds only types that must live for the whole process: theme dictionaries, resource keys, styles, converters and pack resources; controls whose code-behind is limited to binding, dependency-property, routed-event, input and lifecycle mechanics; the ModalWindow and ModelessWindow base types with their owner-handle contracts, and the tool window shells ToolWindowModalShell and ToolWindowModelessShell; tool-specific behaviors, converters and controls under Tools/<TOOL>/; the structural 3D viewport (see Structural Preview); the shared logger factory, scope provider and Serilog provider types; SerilogStack, which coordinates the process-wide logger across Core generations; the ambient Revit application slot, RevitApplicationContextSlot; the asynchronous Revit call timing state, RevitCallGateActionTiming. Production source is under src/dbtools.Presentation, with namespaces dbtools.Presentation.* that follow the folder tree. Compiled tool settings views live under Tools/<TOOL>/ in dbtools.Presentation.Tools.<TOOL> when their code-behind registers WPF dependency properties. ElevationTags and FoundationTags use this form. DialogSuppression and JoistGirderWeight embed markup-only settings views in their tool assemblies as raw XAML. The project lists each Page and EmbeddedResource item; default Compile inclusion owns the code-behind. See Theme System for the two supported settings view forms. Presentation does not reference dbtools.dll, Core, tool types, view models, commands, services or the Revit API. App, Core and the tools may reference Presentation. The standalone assemblies for the merged libraries are not shipped. ColorPickerPopup exposes and binds dependency properties by property path, and popup dismissal updates the stable IsPopupOpen property. ProgressOverlayControl binds to the command that the host supplies. Tool windows Tool views are raw embedded XAML. ToolWindowHost creates a modal or modeless shell, parses the view inside ToolWindowReflectionScope and sets the tool's view model. Core's ToolWindowFactory runs WindowInitializer on the shell first, which installs owner, theme, progress and error handling, and then registers the session. Hosts call session.ShowDialog() or session.Show() and get named controls with session.Require<T>(name). When a session closes or is retired, Presentation tears down bindings, automation roots, resources and callbacks. See Theme System. UI Automation item lifetime Retirement does not clear cached automation peers. In WPF 10.0.0, item peers hold reference-type rows weakly (ItemAutomationPeer._item uses ItemWeakReference, and DataGridCellItemAutomationPeer._item is weak), and teardown cuts the strong column, row-item and DataContext references. Tool items in a DataGrid, ListBox or TreeView, their types and a collectible tool context can therefore be released after retirement, also while a UI Automation client is attached. Rows are held strongly, and a collectible tool assembly stays loaded, in these cases: the first item cached by a peer store has an unreliable hash code (for example ComponentResourceKey); the store switches to list mode and holds every later key strongly; the items are boxed value types; the ItemAutomationPeerKeepsItsItemAlive switch makes _item strong; a UI Automation client holds an item element, which keeps its control alive through ElementProxy._peer. Enumerating ItemPeersStorage or _WeakRefElementProxyStorage materializes the weak keys, so their contents do not show an owning reference. Resource URIs /dbtools.Presentation;V<PresentationVersion>;component/Resources/Theme.xaml Raw and reloadable XAML declares stable namespaces with assembly=dbtools.Presentation. XAML compiled inside Presentation uses the form without assembly=. See Theme System for URI rules and Assembly Loading Contract for the distribution layout. Tests Project Target Content dbtools.Presentation.Pure.Tests net10.0-windows Presentation behavior without Revit, including the tool-specific behaviors, converters and controls under Tools/<TOOL>/, the tool window host and the logger window view. References Core for the tool window, window runtime and logger window integration fixtures, and every tool assembly for the embedded payload XAML sweep. dbtools.Presentation.Local.Tests net10.0-windows Revit-hosted structural preview fixtures. The projects are under src/dbtools.Presentation/Tests/. The Pure and Local projects use explicit <Compile> membership, and their test files mirror the owner folders. Presentation grants internals to the Pure and Local projects and to the Core test projects, whose fixtures use the internal host boundaries.

developer-guide/projects/sandbox.html.summary: dbtools.Sandbox NAME dbtools.Sandbox - preview tool windows with design-time view models SYNOPSIS Source src/dbtools.Sandbox/ Project dbtools.Sandbox.csproj Assembly dbtools.Sandbox.dll Entry dbtools.Sandbox.App.Startup.SandboxEntry DESCRIPTION dbtools.Sandbox is a Windows WPF application. The dbtools UI Sandbox catalog groups previews by the manifest group and labels each button with the displayName. Select a button to open its preview. See Sandbox Validator for candidate requirements, startup and headless validation. STRUCTURE Paths are relative to src/dbtools.Sandbox/. Path Role App/ Contains the entry point, option parser and WPF application. Composition/ Creates the Sandbox runtime and window sessions. Features/WindowCatalog/ Lists the windows and launches previews. Runtime/ Configures logging and the default window owner mode. Validation/ Checks product metadata and windows. CONTRACTS The project references Core and Presentation with Private="false" and ExcludeAssets="runtime". Sandbox loads both from the selected year. SandboxCatalog discovers sandboxWindows entries in the manifests embedded in App. Each entry names the raw XAML resource and its design-time view model. See Sandbox Integration for the registration rules. SandboxWindowFactory constructs the view model with its parameterless constructor and creates a ToolWindowHost session. If the view model implements IToolWindowSandboxComposer, the factory calls ComposeView after it creates the session. WindowStaticRuntimeConfigurator sets the default owner mode to Unowned. FLOW For a manual preview, use a promoted Revit 2026 distribution on Windows with Revit 2026 installed. Run the commands from the checkout root. pwsh -NoProfile -File build.ps1 BuildSandbox -y 2026 .\.artifacts\sandbox\Release\2026\net10.0-windows\dbtools.Sandbox.exe ` --dist-dir .artifacts\dist\Release\2026 DATA BuildSandbox writes to .artifacts/sandbox/<Configuration>/<year>/net10.0-windows/. TESTS Select the dbtools.Sandbox.Pure.Tests fixtures with the SANDBOX tool key. See Test Pipeline. Area Fixtures Startup CLIOptionsTests, DistributionPathResolverTests, SandboxCandidateTests, HeadlessUISuppressionTests Runtime AppRuntimeTests, SandboxLogTests, WindowStaticRuntimeConfiguratorTests Catalog WindowCatalogEntryViewModelTests, WindowCatalogWindowViewModelTests Validation diagnostics BindingErrorListenerTests, XamlParseExceptionFormatterTests See the headless acceptance test for coverage of packaged candidates. developer-guide/reference/build.html.title: Build commands | dbtools
developer-guide/reference/build.html.summary: Build commands NAME build.sh, build.ps1 - build the product and its test assemblies SYNOPSIS ./build.sh [TARGET] [OPTION]... pwsh -NoProfile -File build.ps1 [TARGET] [OPTION]... DESCRIPTION Use build.sh on Linux or WSL and build.ps1 with PowerShell on Windows. Both pass the target and options to build/Build.proj as MSBuild arguments. Both map the public Restore target to _DBT_Restore because MSBuild reserves Restore for package restore. OPTIONS Both wrappers print the full list of targets, options and defaults from build/Usage.txt. ./build.sh --help pwsh -NoProfile -File build.ps1 --help Task Target and options Publish the distribution BuildAll is the default target. Stage a product year Use BuildApp -y YEAR. Add --debug for Debug output. Compile test projects Use BuildTests for Pure, Local and Design Automation. Use BuildSelectedPureTests --TestProjects A,B to compile selected Pure projects. Package the Autodesk bundle Use BuildBundle. Pass --candidate-dist DIR to use a promoted distribution. BuildTests and the selected-test targets reject --clean and --DryRun true. Use the standalone Clean target to clear build output first. Clean keeps build/, build-tasks/, dist/, acceptance/, test-results/ and build.json under .artifacts/. It deletes all other entries there, including .artifacts/bin/. It also deletes build bin/ and obj/ directories and *_wpftmp.csproj files left in the source tree. The source scan skips build/, docs/, vendor/, .git/, nested Git checkouts and symbolic links. --Revit2026Dir and --Revit2027Dir select the installed metadata files for validation. The default reference source is the Revit API packages. EXIT STATUS The Exit status paragraph of ./build.sh --help (build/Usage.txt) lists the exit codes. ENVIRONMENT Variable Effect DOTNET Selects a dotnet executable if it has the pinned SDK. DBT_BUILD_SERVERS In build.sh, 1 enables compiler and MSBuild servers scoped to the invocation. Set 0 to disable them. The default is 1. PowerShell builds run with servers disabled. DBT_MSBUILD_MAX_CPU_COUNT Sets the MSBuild CPU count for child graphs. The default is 2. DBT_BUILD_CONSOLE_LOG Sets the destination for the copy of the latest detailed log. FILES Path Use global.json Pins the .NET SDK. ~/.dotnet/pinned-sdk-<version>/ Holds the verified SDK when a system installation lacks the pinned version. .artifacts/build/<build-id>/ Holds the detailed console.log and child build binlogs. .artifacts/build/console.log Default path for the copy of the latest run log. .artifacts/bundle/dbtools.bundle Autodesk bundle from BuildBundle. .artifacts/bundle/installer-defines.json Supplies the bundle path, product files, version and years to the installer compiler. EXAMPLES Use --candidate-dist with --DryRun to check a promoted distribution and skip writing the bundle. ./build.sh BuildBundle --candidate-dist .artifacts/dist/Release --DryRun On Windows, use Inno Setup 6.7.1 or later in the 6.x series. Build the bundle, then compile .artifacts/release-assets/dbtools-Setup-<version>.exe. pwsh -NoProfile -File build.ps1 BuildBundle pwsh -NoProfile -File .github/scripts/compile-installer.ps1 SEE ALSO Build Pipeline, Build troubleshooting, Test Pipeline

developer-guide/tools/common/gm-producti.title: GM Production Contracts | dbtools
developer-guide/tools/common/gm-producti.summary: GM Production Contracts These Global Mapper (GM) behaviors are performance or correctness requirements. Each section names the source that implements the contract and the effect of breaking it. A change to a contract is a product change; update this page with it. See Global Mapper for the tool design. Paths are relative to src/Tools/Common/GM/. Usage index sampling cap Features/Usage/Revit/Operations/Indexing/UsageIndexSource.Families.cs, QuerySampleInstanceIdsBySymbol The usage index samples one family instance per family type (symbol), at most 2500 instances (MaxSampleInstances in UsageIndexSource.cs). It streams view-independent (model) instances first and returns as soon as it has 2250 samples. When the model instances give fewer than 2250 samples, it adds view-owned instances up to the cap. The view collector applies visibility in each eligible owner view. The active view is visited first when eligible. Unbounded iteration scales with views times instances: a project with 200 views and 50,000 instances stalls for minutes. Style, body material and paint geometry Features/Usage/Revit/Operations/Indexing/StyleMaterial/UsageStyleMaterialCollector.cs, QueryStyleMaterialUsageChunk Style and material usage share the sample and element lookup. Style geometry uses the owning or active view. Body material geometry uses view-independent Fine detail. Both include non-visible geometry. Style and non-column body reads use symbol geometry when the placed instance returns none. Column body reads use original instance geometry. Eligible instances use a separate project paint read of visible placed faces with references enabled. Revit can wrap a placed family's own geometry in a GeometryInstance with a different symbol ID, or flatten an embedded family's solids into the placed type. The walker treats a matching placed-symbol wrapper as direct usage. Family browsing and Material planning also walk placed shared subcomponents exposed by Revit. They reuse each child type's material evidence within the query and read the material IDs of each placement. Their material paths follow the subcomponent hierarchy. The project usage index attributes each separately sampled shared instance to its own family for verification. Flattened embedded solids can supply material usage without an observable nested path. Object Style and Material batches discover nested documents even when the placed sample shows only direct usage. A complete Deep Scan that establishes the family has no children limits the edit to the root. For a Material mapping, GM opens eligible children when the parent document contains the source material name or a category or subcategory in that document resolves to the source through project Object Styles. This check applies to shared and embedded children. ApplyPlanAsync_ReplacesMaterialFromAnIndependentlyReloadedSharedChild checks that Edit Family exposes a reloaded shared child's new material in a direct parent and through one embedded intermediate. For an eligible shared child already loaded in the project, GM opens the current project definition. Discovery caches material matches and misses and closes a document that has no eligible operations when its check ends. GM reports a failed close and retries once during batch cleanup. Replacement verification uses the write scope Features/CommitReview/Verification/CommitReviewPlanVerifier.cs, VerifyAfterApplyAsync GM discovers all family documents needed by a batch before applying changes. A batch whose discovery fails contributes no operations to shared children. GM reports an error on any family mapping that skipped a child because of a project mapping whose discovery subsequently failed. Successful batches capture the original references in each planned family document. The writers read each changed reference back and report write and reload failures. A protected group reference stays in place and appears in the report as a warning. Commit Review checks that each result matches its planned operation and owner family. Commit Review checks the remaining restylable curves for project Line Styles. It checks sampled Object Style and Material usage across the project for a project mapping. It samples every placed type in owner families, planned batch roots and families named by write receipts or incomplete-write warnings. A family mapping checks usage in its owner, its batch roots and the families named by its incomplete-write warnings. Commit Review reports a verification warning when the project sample reaches its limit. Family Material verification reads the shared subcomponents of every placement of an owner or batch root. It merges material usage by root and shared family path. GM reads body geometry at most once per child symbol and checks each occurrence's effective body materials where Revit reports them. If Revit cannot establish the body materials of another occurrence, verification reports that path as unverified and rolls back the attempt. Verification omits paths through excluded families and families reported as skipped for scope. Separate placements of a shared family do not contribute to this check. For Object Style and Material, a write that introduces an outgoing source explains its remaining use only in a family named by the incoming receipt. Each outgoing operation planned for that family must also report a change there. If no outgoing work was planned for a family in scope, verification requires a complete planning sample or a completed Deep Scan with no partial results for that family. For a shared child on a Material mapping's path, an incoming receipt requires a successful outgoing receipt or pre-Apply evidence that the child did not use the outgoing source. An incomplete-write warning blocks the explanation for the family it names. Source-absence warnings describe an individual document and leave the verification check in place. Receipts record host parameter writes and reloaded family edits. A root receives credit for its own edits and edits to its embedded families. A shared child and its embedded families contribute changes under the shared child's project ID. A root reload can publish a shared child for the first time or change the child's element ID. GM resolves shared children by name and category after the last reload. A family edit receipt records the planning ID when one exists and the final project ID for a newly loaded child. The reload map resolves earlier IDs to their current IDs. An equivalent shared mapping contributes one write, credited to the operation that made it. A group skip explains the matching operation and family when the receipt reports no incomplete write there. Project Material replacement captures writable host type and instance parameters before family and type writes. A family Material mapping captures writable parameters on the owner family's placed instances and checks that they still belong to that family when it writes. Revit can return an old value for a placed instance parameter until the transaction commits. The writer reads each accepted write back after commit. It reports the fatal HostMaterialWriteNotRetained error if the value differs from the target. A parameter already set to the planned target needs no write and adds no host count. Other changed values and parameters that become unwritable fail the rule. Missing captured elements or parameters are reported as warnings. Material batch planning combines geometry evidence from one placed instance per type of each affected family. A family-owned Material or Object Style mapping takes precedence over the project choice for that source. The same family can exclude the project choice by clearing Apply on its row. The project operation excludes those families from its work and verification. A shared child follows its own mapping or Apply exclusion. A family-scoped operation also skips a shared child when project traversal reaches that child for the same source. GM checks material references in these skipped families only to report the skip. An inspection failure in a skipped shared child is a warning. GM reports a skip when the inspection finds source use. A mapping can still update host parameters when there is no evidence for a family edit. Planned family edits require a batch result. Paint applied in the project remains in place. For a family Material mapping, the writer warns about painted instances and verification checks unpainted material usage. Project Material mappings also check project paint for remaining source usage. Revit can return an empty GetMaterialIds(true) collection for a column with paint on a face. A saved face reference can also fail to resolve after painting changes the instance geometry. A painted column's GetMaterialIds(false) and placed faces can include the project finish. The material walker reads column body materials from FamilyInstance.GetOriginalGeometry, which retains the placed instance values and excludes post-processing such as joins. When Revit supplies no original geometry, GM checks the placed geometry for solid faces. A column without solid faces contributes no body geometry. Placed solid faces without an original representation or a Revit read failure report the column and document identity. The body pass reads solid faces at Fine detail. Materials present only in meshes, other detail levels or takeoff data can be absent from this column index. The walker reads project paint from visible surfaces of the placed geometry through Document.GetPaintedMaterial. The surface reference must belong to the placed family instance. GM requests referenced geometry for columns, masses, in-place families, and model instances with top-level solids or modified geometry. A top-level solid can represent geometry that Revit owns on the placement. Host capture requests paint for families with a scoped source. Separate reads allow a material used for both the body and paint to appear in both indexes. Revit API geometry instances · Revit family instance geometry · Revit original instance geometry · Revit project paint · Paint on family instances with their own geometry Capture reports named warnings for shared nested type values, read-only material references and material set By Category. In a placed family, Revit resolves a By Category solid using the existing project Object Styles subcategory of the same name. An unassigned subcategory inherits the project category material. Edit Family can expose that project material in the parent document's material table. Capture checks the element's assignment for By Category use. For a form without a subcategory, capture uses the owning family's category. A missing material ID and InvalidElementId represent an unset material on an associated material parameter. Family capture checks type assignments for placed types. It also checks instance defaults when the mapping's host capture excludes that family's instances. Host capture uses each covered project instance's effective parameter value and body material usage. It uses original geometry for columns. A covered instance whose override selects a concrete material contributes no By Category warning from its family default. Capture and write warnings name the edited document's project family when known. Warnings for embedded documents name the enclosing project family, and the path identifies the specific document. A skipped shared type projection names the shared family because loading the parent with FamilySource.Project keeps the project's shared type. A newly loaded shared family receives its project ID in these diagnostics after the final reload. A failed nested reload keeps that child out of the set of changed identities for the parent's reload. A nonshared type projection that matches a child edit receives the child value during reload. A different parent override retains its value. GM reports NoWritableMaterialReferences when the document's own non-nested elements use the source and capture finds neither a writable reference nor another warning. Remaining unexplained usage fails verification. One instance for parameter discovery Features/Families/Revit/FamilyScanner.ParameterNames.cs, QueryMappableParamNamesForFamily Parameter-name discovery reads the parameters of every type of the family and of one instance. Parameter definitions are family-level, so every instance has the same definitions; scanning more instances adds cost and no data. Deep scan runs only on request Features/DeepScan/Workflow/DeepScanWorkflow.cs A deep scan opens family documents with EditFamily, which takes seconds per family. It runs only from a user action. Scan Family scans one family. A project scan uses the loaded project family inventory. Deep Scan Unscanned scans eligible zero-instance families across the project after confirmation. Background prewarm reads the deep scan cache. Family and type edits and deletions invalidate affected evidence. Instance changes invalidate evidence when the inventory shows a change in placement counts. Commit Review tracks family changes until Revit settles each attempt and the session group. It discards pending family changes after confirmed rollbacks and reads LastFinalizationOutcome when settling the session group. See GM specification. Parameter discovery filter Revit/ParameterDiscovery/ParameterDiscoveryEligibility.cs Discovery excludes read-only parameters, built-in parameters (InternalDefinition with a valid BuiltInParameter) and blank definition names. It does not filter on UserModifiable, because Revit can report a parameter that the API can write as not user-modifiable. Removing the read-only or built-in filter offers parameters that cannot be written or should not be mapped. Adding a UserModifiable filter hides valid mapping targets. Simple style canonicalization UsageStyleMaterialCollector.RecordStyle; Features/Usage/Revit/Operations/Indexing/UsageIndexSource.StyleMaterial.cs, BuildStyleCanonicalizationMap Style usage records the raw style ID and its canonical projection ID only. Recording every equivalent alias multiplies dictionary insertions per geometry object without improving the result. Style maps built once per usage build UsageIndexSource.StyleMaterial.cs, BuildStyleMaterialUsageAsync Style canonicalization, category projection and object-style classification run once per usage build, and their results are passed to each chunk of 25 instances (UsageChunkSize). Rebuilding them per chunk repeats a full FilteredElementCollector scan for every chunk.
